meta.title: Electricity — Class 10 study library
meta.intro: Official-source compilations and original revision material; provenance and limitations remain visible.

coverage.summary: Evidence-led Electricity revision with a partial, explicitly bounded official-source archive. Represented sessions: 2017-18, 2018, 2018-19, 2019-20, 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022, 2022-23, 2023, 2023-24, 2024, 2024-25, 2025, 2025-26, 2026, 2026-27
limitations: Fifteen mixed-source compilations are not fifteen distinct official CBSE chapter papers. Questions are reused across papers with per-question disclosure.
Last-ten-year coverage is bounded by the source inventories below. Downloaded bundles do not imply every year, set, language, supplementary sitting or alternative was analysed.
The cancelled 2021 Class X annual examination must not be represented as a normal annual PYQ sitting. Sample papers are a separate category.
Unverified answers are excluded from printable solution keys. Source images are not automatically verified by rendering.
68 source records were excluded from paper selection by assembly checks; details are in the assembly validation report.

SQP declared scope: Latest ten available sessions, 2017-18 through 2026-27. Official CBSE standard English Science SQPs only; both terms in 2021-22; all qualifying main/internal-choice/accessibility Electricity content. Hindi 2025-26 counterparts downloaded but not separately extracted or audited as independent question sets. Excludes actual board examination papers, competency question banks, additional practice sets and older sessions. Reviewed 11 English SQPs and 11 English marking schemes, 130 + 96 PDF pages. Separate alternatives are not additive.
SQP: English editions exhaustively extracted; Hindi counterparts not compared line-by-line.
SQP: Live downloaded files reflect retrieval on 2026-10-06; cannot prove historical byte versions beyond retained hashes.
SQP: Some official marking schemes contain arithmetic/typographical errors; see record notes.
SQP: 2022-23 Q36 MS omits c and d; c derived answer explicitly distinguished; no official d answer fabricated.
SQP: 2018-19 Q26 meter diagram is displaced beside Q22 in official layout; separate diagram crop retained and relationship documented.

Actual searchable-bank PYQ records by year: 2018: 3 verified questions, 2022: 3 verified questions, 2023: 3 verified questions, 2024: 3 verified questions, 2025: 6 verified questions, 2026: 12 verified questions. All eligible verified records are searchable, including records not selected in papers and genuine one-mark short-answer questions. Other accepted PYQ records lacking original section provenance or resolved choice accounting were held out. The research-bank inventory is broader than this published selection.

Separate PYQ/SQP master PDFs use only the current published verified bank; no expanded audit or exhaustive all-set coverage is claimed. Special39, when present, is additional original competency practice, not official questions or a prediction.

sqp.title: CBSE Class X Science SQP Electricity coverage manifest
sqp.scope: Latest ten available sessions, 2017-18 through 2026-27. Official CBSE standard English Science SQPs only; both terms in 2021-22; all qualifying main/internal-choice/accessibility Electricity content. Hindi 2025-26 counterparts downloaded but not separately extracted or audited as independent question sets. Excludes actual board examination papers, competency question banks, additional practice sets and older sessions.
sqp.record_counting: Separate alternatives/accessibility versions are separate records. Case Q39 2023-24 has two complete alternative versions sharing common subparts. Record marks are NOT additive across alternatives. One mixed Q33(ii) is a self-contained subpart only.
sqp.type_extension: short1 is used for genuine one-mark VSA questions; it prevents falsely classifying these as MCQ. Other types match the requested enumeration.
sqp.source_of_truth: PDFs and source-rendered crop images preserve exact typography and diagrams; text normalizes whitespace/math glyph layout. Official errors are retained and noted.
sqp.verification: Full-page local source/text review by extraction reviewers plus independent parent audit, selected visual diagram checks, complete expected-parent reconciliation and machine validation. Not every text-only MS crop was separately vision-loaded.
sqp.chapter_rule: NCERT Electricity sections 11.6 and 11.7.1 include appliance parallel connection, fuse series placement/protection/melting and rating calculations. These are retained despite overlap with domestic circuits. Earthing, three-pin explanation, wiring conventions, standard circuit rating recall, magnetic field/force/motor/generator/induction are excluded unless a self-contained Electricity-only subpart is separable.

documents.title: Electricity foundations — Class 10
documents.subtitle: Original Class 10 notes — current, circuits, graphs and resistance
documents.description: Detailed foundations with nine original checked worked examples and source-verified Activities 11.1–11.6 from NCERT Chapter 11, Reprint 2026–27.

sections.heading: Scope and source
paragraphs: These original notes explain current, potential difference, resistance, measurements, graphs, wire geometry and resistor networks. All worked examples are newly written teaching examples, not official NCERT or CBSE questions. They make no predictions or guarantees about examinations. Heating, power and examination guidance belong to the companion document.

The reference is NCERT Science, Chapter 11, Electricity, Reprint 2026–27. Citations below use printed textbook pages, not PDF page numbers. The official source throughout is https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf. Explanations and examples are original; activity descriptions are paraphrased. Numerical circuits assume ideal connecting wires and meters, steady current and constant resistor temperature unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: 1. Current: charge crossing a section
paragraphs: Electric current measures how quickly charge passes through a cross-section of a conductor: I = Q/t. Thus Q = It and t = Q/I. For steady current this ratio applies throughout the interval; over an arbitrary interval it gives the average current. Charge is measured in coulombs, C, and time in seconds, s. One ampere means one coulomb passing per second: 1 A = 1 C/s.

A closed conducting path is needed for sustained current in a simple cell-and-resistor circuit. Opening its only path stops current. In metallic wires electrons move opposite to conventional current. Through the external circuit, conventional current runs from the cell’s positive terminal towards its negative terminal. Current is not the number of electrons sitting inside a wire.
Source: NCERT section 11.1, printed pp. 171–172; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 2. Potential difference: work per charge
paragraphs: Potential difference describes work done per unit charge between two points: V = W/Q, so W = VQ. One volt means one joule per coulomb: 1 V = 1 J/C. A 3 V potential difference corresponds to 3 J for every coulomb transferred between the specified points, not 3 C every second.

A cell’s chemical action maintains a potential difference. Its terminals can have a potential difference even when the external circuit is open and current is zero. Therefore voltage and current are different quantities. Always identify the two points meant by a voltage; saying “voltage through the resistor” confuses an across-two-points measurement with current through a component.
Source: NCERT section 11.2, printed pp. 173–174; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 3. Units and conversions before substitution
paragraphs: Convert data before combining formulas. Keep the symbol A for ampere distinct from A used for cross-sectional area; context and units identify the meaning.
Source: NCERT sections 11.1, 11.4 and 11.5, printed pp. 172, 176, 178–180; conversions apply standard SI prefixes. https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.
bullets: 1 minute = 60 s; 2.5 minutes = 150 s.
1 cm = 10⁻² m and 1 mm = 10⁻³ m.
1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m², not 10⁻³ m²: an area conversion squares the length factor.
Resistance uses Ω; resistivity uses Ω m. Neither unit can replace the other.

sections.heading: 4. Meters and circuit interpretation
paragraphs: Insert an ammeter in series with the path whose current is required. Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the two endpoints being compared. An ideal ammeter adds no resistance; an ideal voltmeter draws no current. These are calculation assumptions, not literal descriptions of real instruments. Never connect an ammeter directly across a cell.

Follow connections rather than the shape of the drawing. A junction divides a path; wires crossing without joining do not form a junction. Two resistors are in series only when the same current must pass through both without branching between them. Parallel resistors share both endpoints, even if they look far apart on paper. A bend in an ideal wire does not create a voltage drop.

For supervised low-voltage measurements, open the key before changing connections, check meter polarity and range, and read scales without parallax. Determine the value per division from the marked scale. Use appropriately rated apparatus; these notes do not instruct experiments with mains electricity.

Source: NCERT sections 11.1–11.3, printed pp. 172–175; Activities 11.2 and 11.6, pp. 176–177 and 185–186. Meter idealisations and handling reminders are explanatory additions. https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 5. Resistance and the condition in Ohm’s law
paragraphs: Resistance describes opposition to charge flow. R = V/I, measured in ohms: a conductor has resistance 1 Ω when 1 V across it produces 1 A through it. For a given metallic conductor at constant temperature, Ohm’s law states V ∝ I, giving V = IR with constant R.

Writing V/I for one observation does not prove that resistance stays constant over other observations. Test several pairs while keeping temperature unchanged. A wire that warms appreciably may give changing ratios. At fixed V, doubling R halves I; at fixed R, doubling V doubles I. State what remains fixed before drawing either conclusion. A rheostat changes circuit resistance to regulate current without changing the voltage source.
Source: NCERT section 11.4, printed pp. 175–177; temperature dependence also section 11.5, p. 179. https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 6. Both graph orientations: read the axes first
paragraphs: An ohmic conductor at constant temperature gives a straight line through the origin. “Steeper means greater resistance” is incomplete unless the axes and their units are known. Compare slopes on identical numerical scales, not merely the apparent angle of separately drawn graphs.
Source: NCERT section 11.4, Activity 11.1 and Fig. 11.3, printed pp. 175–176. Reciprocal-axis slopes follow algebraically from V = IR. https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.
bullets: V–I graph: horizontal axis I in A; vertical axis V in V. Slope = ΔV/ΔI = R, in Ω. A steeper line means larger resistance.
I–V graph: horizontal axis V in V; vertical axis I in A. Slope = ΔI/ΔV = 1/R, in A/V. A steeper line means smaller resistance.
Use two widely separated points on a best-fit straight line, subtract coordinates in matching order, and convert mA to A before reporting resistance in Ω.
Small experimental scatter is not automatically failure of Ohm’s law. Check readings and temperature; do not force a clearly curved relationship into a constant-resistance interpretation.

sections.heading: 7. Resistivity, area and diameter
paragraphs: For a uniform wire, R = ρl/A. Resistance depends on length l, cross-sectional area A, material and temperature. Resistivity ρ describes the material at a specified temperature; changing length alone does not change ρ. Rearranging gives ρ = RA/l, whose unit is Ω m.

For the same material at the same temperature, R₂/R₁ = (l₂/l₁)(A₁/A₂). Longer wires resist more when area is fixed; thicker wires resist less when length is fixed. For a circular section, A = πd²/4. Therefore doubling diameter quadruples area and quarters resistance at unchanged length. Doubling area only halves resistance. “Twice as thick” is ambiguous: specify diameter or area.
Source: NCERT section 11.5, printed pp. 177–180, including Eq. 11.10 and the diameter calculation in Example 11.5. https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 8. Stretching a wire: two changes together
paragraphs: For uniform stretching, explicitly assume constant volume, unchanged material resistivity and constant temperature. If length becomes n times its original value, lA = l′A′ gives A′ = A/n. Substitution then gives R′ = ρ(nl)/(A/n) = n²R. For a circular wire, d′ = d/√n.

Do not use R′ = nR: that result holds when area stays fixed, whereas stretching makes the wire thinner. This is a derived application of the NCERT geometry relation, not a claim that every real stretching process preserves resistivity. Cutting a wire into equal pieces is different: each piece keeps the original area but has a shorter length.
Source basis: NCERT section 11.5, Eq. 11.10, printed p. 178; ratio reasoning on p. 180. Constant-volume stretching is an original extension. https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 9. Series resistance: derive before using
paragraphs: Series resistors carry the same current I. The total potential difference equals the sum of individual drops: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃. Applying Ohm’s law gives IRₛ = IR₁ + IR₂ + IR₃; cancelling nonzero I gives Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃.

For positive resistances, the result exceeds every individual resistance. Since V₁ = IR₁ and V₂ = IR₂, V₁/V₂ = R₁/R₂: the larger resistor receives the larger voltage drop. Equal current does not mean equal voltage. Breaking the only series path stops current throughout it.
Source: NCERT section 11.6.1, Activities 11.4–11.5 and Eqs. 11.11–11.14, printed pp. 182–184; broken-path discussion p. 187. https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 10. Parallel resistance and mixed networks
paragraphs: Parallel branches share the same potential difference V. The total current is I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃. Substituting I = V/R gives V/Rₚ = V/R₁ + V/R₂ + V/R₃; cancelling nonzero V gives 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃.

For two resistors only, Rₚ = R₁R₂/(R₁ + R₂). For n identical resistors, Rₚ = R/n. Equivalent resistance is smaller than the smallest positive branch resistance. Since I₁/I₂ = R₂/R₁, the lower-resistance branch carries more current; current does not divide equally unless branch resistances are equal.

In mixed networks, label junctions and reduce one genuine series or parallel group at a time. Find total current, then work backwards to group voltages and branch currents. Do not assign the whole battery voltage to a parallel group that has another resistor in series with it.
Source: NCERT section 11.6.2, printed pp. 185–187, Eqs. 11.15–11.18 and mixed-network Example 11.9. https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 11. Original worked examples: charge and voltage
paragraphs: Example 1 — Charge transfer. A steady current of 240 mA flows for 2.5 minutes. Convert I = 0.240 A and t = 150 s. Then Q = It = 0.240 × 150 = 36 C. Check: 36/150 = 0.240 C/s, recovering the current. Using 2.5 without converting minutes would give the wrong charge.

Example 2 — Work per coulomb. Transferring 0.75 C between two points requires 4.5 J. V = W/Q = 4.5/0.75 = 6 V. For 2 C between the same points, W = VQ = 6 × 2 = 12 J. Check: 12/2 = 6 J/C. More transferred charge increases total work, not the fixed potential difference.
Formula sources: NCERT sections 11.1–11.2, printed pp. 172–174; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 12. Original worked examples: resistance and graph slopes
paragraphs: Example 3 — Milliampere conversion. A resistor carries 4 mA at 6 V. I = 0.004 A, so R = 6/0.004 = 1500 Ω = 1.5 kΩ. At 3 V and unchanged temperature, I = 3/1500 = 0.002 A = 2 mA. Check: IR = 0.002 × 1500 = 3 V.

Example 4 — One resistor, two plots. Points on a straight line are (I, V) = (0.10 A, 1.5 V) and (0.30 A, 4.5 V). With V vertical, slope = (4.5 − 1.5)/(0.30 − 0.10) = 15 Ω. With I vertical, slope = 0.20/3.0 = 1/15 A/V; its reciprocal is 15 Ω. Check: both pointwise V/I ratios equal 15 Ω.
Formula source: NCERT section 11.4, printed pp. 175–176; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 13. Original worked examples: wire geometry
paragraphs: Example 5 — Find resistivity. A uniform wire has R = 3 Ω, l = 1.5 m and A = 0.20 mm² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ m². Thus ρ = RA/l = (3 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁷)/1.5 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. Check: ρl/A returns 3 Ω. This hypothetical value is not assigned to a named material.

Example 6 — Diameter versus stretching. A wire initially has resistance 12 Ω. A separate wire of the same material, temperature and length but twice its diameter has resistance 12/4 = 3 Ω. Instead, stretching the original uniformly to 1.5 times its length at constant volume, temperature and resistivity gives R′ = 1.5² × 12 = 27 Ω. Check: A′ = A/1.5, so the geometry multiplier is 1.5/(1/1.5) = 2.25.
Formula source: NCERT section 11.5, printed pp. 178–180; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 14. Original worked examples: complete networks
paragraphs: Example 7 — Series. Connect 4 Ω and 8 Ω in series across 6 V. Rₛ = 12 Ω and I = 6/12 = 0.5 A through each resistor. Voltage drops are 0.5 × 4 = 2 V and 0.5 × 8 = 4 V. Check: 2 + 4 = 6 V and 2:4 = 4:8.

Example 8 — Parallel. Connect 8 Ω and 24 Ω across 6 V. Rₚ = (8 × 24)/(8 + 24) = 6 Ω. Branch currents are 6/8 = 0.75 A and 6/24 = 0.25 A. Total current = 1 A. Check: V/I = 6 Ω, below 8 Ω, and branch currents sum correctly.

Example 9 — Mixed. A 3 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 12 Ω across 7 V. The pair equals 72/18 = 4 Ω; total resistance is 7 Ω and total current is 1 A. The series resistor drops 3 V, leaving 4 V across both branches. Branch currents are 4/6 = 2/3 A and 4/12 = 1/3 A. Check: branch currents sum to 1 A and voltage drops sum to 7 V.
Formula sources: NCERT sections 11.6.1–11.6.2, printed pp. 182–187; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.

sections.heading: 15. Activities 11.1–11.6: procedure, observation, meaning
paragraphs: These are paraphrased source-based expectations, not measurements performed for these notes. Actual readings depend on apparatus and uncertainty. Change connections with the key open and use teacher-supervised low-voltage apparatus.
Official reference for every activity: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.
bullets: Activity 11.1, section 11.4, p. 175; interpretation p. 176: measure I through and V across a nichrome wire using one, two, three and four 1.5 V cells successively. V/I should be approximately constant and the graph straight through the origin when temperature stays constant. Record measured voltage, not just nominal cell totals.

Activity 11.2, section 11.4, pp. 176–177: replace the component in gap XY successively with nichrome wire, a torch bulb and the listed 10 W bulb, using four dry cells. Different current readings indicate differing opposition to current. Do not invent a universal ranking without component data. Remove the key after each reading.

Activity 11.3, section 11.5, pp. 177–178: compare the original nichrome wire with twice its length, a thicker wire of the original length, and copper of matching length and area. NCERT reports half current on doubling length, increased current with thickness, and a change with material. The half-current comparison assumes essentially unchanged voltage across the test wire.

Activity 11.4, section 11.6.1, p. 182: move the ammeter between positions in a three-resistor series path. The reading remains the same: current is common throughout the series combination, not consumed by successive resistors.

Activity 11.5, section 11.6.1, p. 183: measure voltage across the whole series combination, compare it with battery terminal voltage, then measure each resistor separately. Observe V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃; unequal resistors need not have equal drops.

Activity 11.6, section 11.6.2, pp. 185–186: measure total current and voltage for three parallel resistors; then measure each branch current with the ammeter in that branch. Voltage is common and I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃, not necessarily three equal currents.

sections.heading: 16. Misconceptions to replace
paragraphs: Source basis: NCERT sections 11.1–11.6, printed pp. 171–187, especially pp. 173, 176, 178–179, 182–186; https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf.
bullets: “Current gets used up.” Charge continues through a steady series path; current is unchanged between resistors. Energy transfer is a different idea.
“A battery always supplies the same current.” Current depends on the connected resistance as well as terminal voltage.
“Zero current means zero voltage everywhere.” An open cell-powered circuit can retain a terminal potential difference.
“A thick wire has lower resistivity.” Geometry changes resistance; resistivity belongs to the material at its temperature.
“Resistance always equals graph slope.” Only a graph with V vertical and I horizontal has slope R.
“Adding resistors always increases resistance.” Adding a series resistor increases it; adding a positive parallel branch decreases it.

sections.heading: Official curriculum scope and assessment limitation
paragraphs: CBSE Science (086), Class X, 2026–27, PDF p.6 Unit IV lists electric current, potential difference, resistance, resistivity, Ohm’s law, resistor combinations, heating and power. Practical 4 on PDF p.7 covers V–I measurements; practical 5 on PDF p.8 covers series and parallel equivalent resistance. Source: https://cbseacademic.nic.in/web_material/CurriculumMain27/SecPart1/Science_SecP1_2026-27.pdf

documents.title: Electricity applications: heating, power, energy and exam preparation

sections.heading: A1. Scope and source map
paragraphs: These original Class 10 notes extend the foundations note through applications, assumptions and interpretation.

Source: NCERT Science, Chapter 11, Electricity, Reprint 2026–27. Section 11.7 begins on printed page 188; its derivation continues on 189; section 11.7.1 occupies page 190. Section 11.8 actually starts on page 191 and continues onto 192, not 190. All page references below are printed pages. Official source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — sections 11.7–11.8, pp. 188–192.

All worked examples, experimental datasets, self-test questions and revision plans here are original teaching material, not official questions or marking schemes. Suggested priorities are not predictions: there are no invented prediction probabilities and no guarantee about examination content or marks.

sections.heading: A2. Derive Joule’s heating law, not just its final line
paragraphs: Potential difference is work done per unit charge, so transferring charge Q through voltage V requires electrical energy W = VQ. For a steady current, Q = It. Substitution gives W = VIt. In a purely resistive device, electrical energy becomes heat, hence H = VIt. Using V = IR gives H = (IR)It = I²Rt.

Thus heat depends on the square of current, resistance and duration. State the quantities held constant whenever describing proportionality. Doubling current gives four times the heat only when R and t remain unchanged. Doubling time doubles heat only when the electrical operating conditions remain unchanged.

Use amperes, ohms and seconds to obtain joules. Here W denotes work in the derivation; the unit symbol W elsewhere means watt. Do not assume that all input energy becomes useful heating in every appliance. Electrical energy may also produce motion or light; even in a heater, some heat escapes to the surroundings.
Source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — section 11.7, pp. 188–189, equations 11.19–11.21.

sections.heading: A3. Fixed current versus fixed voltage: the decisive comparison
paragraphs: The statement “more resistance produces more heat” is incomplete. First identify what the source or connection keeps unchanged. Substituting I = V/R into H = I²Rt also gives H = V²t/R. These are equivalent expressions, not conflicting laws.

For a cord and heating element carrying the same current, the element’s greater resistance produces more electrical heating. Whether a part glows also depends on its temperature, dimensions and heat loss; resistance alone is not a complete temperature argument.
Source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — section 11.7, pp. 188–190. The fixed-voltage comparison is an algebraic consequence of the cited equations.
bullets: Fixed I and t: H = I²Rt, so a larger resistance produces more heat. Comparing parts carrying the same current uses this condition.
Fixed V and t: H = V²t/R, so a larger resistance produces less heat because the current decreases.
Fixed R and t: doubling V doubles I and makes heat four times larger.
If temperature changes R appreciably, a calculation using one unchanged resistance is only an approximation; see A8.

sections.heading: A4. Useful heating and material choice
paragraphs: An iron transfers heat to fabric; a toaster heats food; a kettle heats water. Their purpose makes electrical heating useful rather than merely an unwanted loss. Heating elements commonly use alloys with relatively high resistivity that do not oxidise readily at high temperatures. Avoid saying that every high-resistance material is suitable: the element must also tolerate operating conditions.

An incandescent filament must become hot enough to emit light without melting. NCERT identifies tungsten’s high melting point and describes an inactive gas filling that helps prolong filament life. Much of the input power appears as heat rather than visible light. This explanation concerns filament lamps, not every type of lamp.
Source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — section 11.5, p. 179; section 11.7.1, p. 190.

sections.heading: A5. Power and appliance ratings
paragraphs: Power measures the rate of energy transfer: P = E/t. For electrical input, P = VI. For a resistor, substitution gives P = I²R = V²/R. Power is measured in watts; 1 W = 1 J/s and 1 kW = 1000 W. Heat and power are different: a modest power maintained for a long time can deliver substantial energy.

A rating such as “240 V, 1200 W” specifies operation at the stated voltage. It gives rated current I = P/V and operating resistance R = V²/P for the resistive model. It does not mean that the device consumes 1200 joules in total, nor that its power remains 1200 W at every voltage.

At another voltage, use P = V²/R only if resistance is assumed unchanged. Real operating resistance can depend on temperature. Nameplate power also does not establish how many hours an appliance is actively drawing that power.
Source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — section 11.7, p. 189; section 11.8, p. 191.

sections.heading: A6. Energy, meter units and cost
paragraphs: Choose the unit route before substituting. Power in watts multiplied by time in seconds gives joules. Power in kilowatts multiplied by time in hours gives kilowatt-hours. A kilowatt-hour is energy, not power, and is commonly called one electricity “unit”.

Unless stated otherwise, a classroom cost problem assumes a constant tariff and omits taxes, standing charges and tariff slabs. A cycling appliance may draw its rated power only during part of the elapsed time. Do not invent an operating fraction when none is supplied.
Source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — section 11.8, pp. 191–192.
bullets: Joules to kWh: divide by 3.6 × 10⁶. kWh to joules: multiply by 3.6 × 10⁶.
Energy charge = energy in kWh × tariff per kWh. Keep currency units in the calculation.
For several appliances, calculate each energy contribution and add them. Use actual operating time, not simply time plugged in.

sections.heading: A7. Eight checked original worked examples
paragraphs: These examples assume steady conditions unless a change is explicitly described. The amounts and tariffs are invented for practice, not taken from official questions. Formula source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — section 11.7, pp. 188–189; section 11.8, pp. 191–192.
bullets: Example 1 — timed heating: A 12 Ω resistor carries 1.5 A for 4 minutes. Convert t = 240 s. H = I²Rt = 1.5² × 12 × 240 = 6480 J. Check: P = 27 W, and 27 × 240 = 6480 J. Leaving time as 4 would understate heat sixtyfold.

Example 2 — same resistors, different constraints: Compare 5 Ω and 10 Ω for 30 s. At a fixed 2 A, their heats are 600 J and 1200 J. Connected separately across 10 V, their heats are 600 J and 300 J. The ordering reverses because the second comparison fixes voltage, not current.

Example 3 — reading a rating: An ideal heater is rated 240 V, 1200 W. I = 1200/240 = 5 A; R = 240²/1200 = 48 Ω. At 120 V with unchanged R, P = 120²/48 = 300 W and I = 2.5 A. Halving voltage quarters power under this assumption.

Example 4 — kettle operating cost: A 1.8 kW kettle runs for 8 minutes daily for 25 days. Total time = 200/60 h. E = 1.8 × 200/60 = 6 kWh = 21.6 × 10⁶ J. At an assumed ₹7.50/kWh, energy charge = ₹45. No additional bill charges are included.

Example 5 — a small mixed-use bill: Four 9 W lamps operate 5 h/day, and a 60 W fan operates 6 h/day, for 30 days. Lamps use 0.036 × 5 × 30 = 5.4 kWh; fan uses 0.060 × 6 × 30 = 10.8 kWh. Total = 16.2 kWh; at ₹6/kWh, charge = ₹97.20.

Example 6 — reverse calculation from heat: A 16 Ω resistor produces 7200 J in 5 minutes. I² = H/(Rt) = 7200/(16 × 300) = 1.5 A². Current magnitude I = √1.5 ≈ 1.225 A; V = IR ≈ 19.60 V. Check using unrounded values: P = 24 W and Pt = 7200 J.

Example 7 — energy from transferred charge: During a steady transfer, 360 C passes through a resistor across 24 V in 3 minutes. H = VQ = 8640 J. Independently, I = 360/180 = 2 A; P = VI = 48 W; H = 48 × 180 = 8640 J. Charge is not measured in joules.

Example 8 — elapsed time versus active time: A thermostatically controlled 1.5 kW heater is on for 40% of a 5 h period. Given that fraction, active time = 2 h and E = 3 kWh = 10.8 MJ. At ₹8/kWh, the energy charge is ₹24. Assuming uninterrupted heating would incorrectly give 7.5 kWh.

sections.heading: A8. Experiment analysis: ideal relations and real temperature effects
paragraphs: Use only a teacher-supervised low-voltage heating setup, never a mains experiment. Measure current through the element and voltage across it; record heating time and the temperature change of a fixed amount of water. Keep the container, initial temperature, immersion depth and stirring procedure comparable. Let equipment cool before handling or repeating a run.

An ideal comparison might use R = 10 Ω and t = 60 s. At 0.50 A, calculated electrical heat is 150 J; at 1.00 A, it is 600 J. These are illustrative predictions, not measured classroom results. Doubling current predicts four times the electrical heat, but does not automatically prove a fourfold thermometer rise.

Some energy warms the container and element; some escapes to air. Longer or hotter runs can lose different amounts. Uneven stirring, delayed thermometer readings and instrument resolution also affect observations. Repeat trials, compare their spread and report disagreement rather than altering readings to match theory.

Temperature can change resistance itself. For an illustrative fixed 6 V supply, readings of 0.60 A initially and 0.50 A later imply R changing from 10 Ω to 12 Ω and power falling from 3.6 W to 3.0 W. These are hypothetical readings, not reported measurements. A cold resistance would therefore overestimate sustained power in this example; do not generalise its direction to every material.

Record V and I during each run; for substantial changes, estimate energy over short intervals using each interval’s VI and duration, then add. No temperature-coefficient formula is needed. NCERT explicitly limits the constant-resistance relation to unchanged temperature and notes that resistance varies with temperature; it supplies no quantitative temperature model here.
Source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — section 11.4, p. 176; section 11.5, p. 179; section 11.7.1, p. 190. The protocol and interpretation above are original guidance.

sections.heading: A9. Essential formula revision with section anchors
paragraphs: Official source for these revision anchors: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — exact sections and printed pages are given in each bullet.
bullets: A2: W = VQ; Q = It; resistive heat H = VIt = I²Rt. NCERT section 11.7, pp. 188–189.
A3: H = V²t/R for a resistor; identify fixed I or fixed V before comparing. NCERT section 11.7, pp. 188–189, with algebraic substitution.
A5: P = E/t = VI; resistive forms P = I²R = V²/R. Rating relations I = P/V and R = V²/P follow by rearrangement. NCERT section 11.8, p. 191.
A6: E = Pt; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; energy charge = kWh × tariff. NCERT section 11.8, pp. 191–192.
A8: constant-R calculations require attention to temperature. NCERT section 11.4, p. 176; section 11.5, p. 179.

sections.heading: A10. Misconceptions and quick repairs
paragraphs: Source: https://ncert.nic.in/textbook/pdf/jesc111.pdf — section 11.7, pp. 188–190; section 11.8, p. 191. These repairs apply the source relations rather than reproduce official answers.
bullets: “Higher wattage always uses more energy.” Compare power multiplied by operating time, not power alone.
“kW/h and kWh mean the same.” Write kWh for energy: multiplication by hours, not division.
“Higher resistance always heats more.” Name the controlled quantity; return to A3.
“A watt is a joule.” A watt is a joule per second.
“Electrons are used up.” Energy is transferred; electrons are not consumed as fuel.
“The calculated resistor heat all enters the water.” Separate electrical input from the portion reaching the intended object.

sections.heading: A11. Exam method and partial-mark guidance
paragraphs: Read the required quantity first. List known values with units; convert minutes to seconds for joules, or to hours for kWh. Select a relation containing the unknown and available data. Write the symbolic equation before substitution, show one clear calculation line, and finish with the quantity and unit.

For comparisons, state the common voltage or current before the ratio. For explanations, connect condition, equation and conclusion. For derivations, retain the steps VQ, Q = It, H = VIt and V = IR instead of jumping directly to the result.

Clear working makes correct intermediate reasoning visible and may support partial credit even after an arithmetic slip. This is study guidance, not an official rubric: marks depend on the question and its marking scheme. If stuck, write a relevant relation and unit conversion, then return later. Do not manufacture missing data. Finally check whether the numerical size and direction of change are plausible.

sections.heading: A12. A realistic one-week revision plan
paragraphs: Allow about 40 minutes daily, with a short break when needed. Begin each session with five minutes of closed-book recall and finish by recording one error and its correction. Adapt the workload to your timetable rather than sacrificing sleep.

During the final 24 hours, use one short session for formulas and one for your error log. Recheck fixed-current versus fixed-voltage reasoning and time conversions. Avoid a new collection of speculative questions. Prepare required materials, stop heavy study early and protect normal sleep; a brief final recall is enough.
bullets: Day 1: Read A2 and reconstruct the derivation twice without copying. Explain every symbol aloud.
Day 2: Study A3–A4; redo Example 2 and explain why its ordering reverses.
Day 3: Practise ratings using A5 and Examples 1, 3 and 6. Check units and assumptions.
Day 4: Use A6 and Examples 4, 5, 7 and 8. Practise both energy-unit routes.
Day 5: Analyse A8. List controlled variables, likely errors and what changing V/I reveals.
Day 6: Attempt A13 closed-book in 15 minutes; use remaining time to repair weak reasoning.
Day 7: Revisit errors, reproduce A9 from memory and complete two previously missed examples unaided.

sections.heading: A13. Original self-test and answers
paragraphs: Try these without looking back. Award yourself completion only when you can explain the condition or unit, not merely recognise a number.
Review A3 for comparisons, A5 for ratings, A6 for conversions and A8 for experiments.
bullets: Test 1: Current through an unchanged resistor becomes three times larger for the same duration. What happens to heat? Answer: nine times larger, because H depends on I² at fixed R and t.
Test 2: At fixed voltage and duration, resistance doubles. Answer: heat halves; current also halves.
Test 3: A 75 W device operates for 2 h. Answer: 150 Wh = 0.15 kWh = 540000 J.
Test 4: A 200 V, 800 W ideal heater operates at its rating. Answer: I = 4 A; R = 50 Ω.
Test 5: Convert 9 × 10⁶ J to units and calculate the energy charge at ₹6.40/unit. Answer: 2.5 kWh and ₹16.

Test 6: At unchanged voltage, current decreases during warming. What should you check? Answer: calculate V/I at each reading; an increase indicates increased resistance. Check source stability and contacts before attributing the change entirely to temperature.

sections.heading: Official curriculum scope and assessment limitation
paragraphs: CBSE Science (086), Class X, 2026–27, PDF p.6 Unit IV lists electric current, potential difference, resistance, resistivity, Ohm’s law, resistor combinations, heating and power. Practical 4 on PDF p.7 covers V–I measurements; practical 5 on PDF p.8 covers series and parallel equivalent resistance. questions.text:
(i) Consider a conductor of resistance ‘R’, length ‘L’, thickness‘d’ and resistivity ‘ρ’. Now this conductor is cut into four equal parts. What will be the new resistivity of each of these parts? Why?
(ii) Find the resistance if all of these parts are connected in:

(b) Series

questions.notes: All dependent subparts retained in one 5-mark record, including both (ii)(a) and (ii)(b). Marking-scheme answer spans PDF pages 6–7.
questions.answer: (i) Resistivity will not change as it depends on the nature of the material of the conductor. (ii) Each part has length L/4; ρ and A are constant. R = ρL/A; resistance of each part = R/4. (a) In parallel, equivalent resistance = R/16 Ω. (b) In series, equivalent resistance = R Ω. (iii) P = V²/R. At a given voltage, the parallel combination has smaller equivalent resistance and therefore consumes more power.

questions.text:
In the given circuit, A, B, C and D are four lamps connected with a battery of 60V.

Attempt either option A or B.
A.

(ii) Value of the resistance R₂.

questions.notes: Source-verified against complete local text/coordinates and question crops; diagram-dependent and image-only formula evidence visually checked. Layout whitespace and mathematical glyphs normalized; wording/known source errors retained. Answer text is a source-faithful linear transcription; original layout is in answer evidence.
questions.answer:
A.
(i) p.d. across 4 Ω resistor = p.d. Across R₂ as both are in parallel. (0.5)
1.5 (A) × 4 (Ω) = 6 V (0.5)
(ii) Total Current through 4 Ω and R₂ = 2.0 A (given).
Current through 4 Ω = 1.5 A (given) (0.5)
Hence current through R₂ = 2-1.5= 0.5 A
Using Ohm’s law for R₂ we get (0.5)
6 V= 0.5 A x R₂
Hence R₂ = 6/0.5 = 12 Ω (0.5)
(iii) p.d. across R₁ = Total p.d. - (p.d. across R₂) - (p.d. across 2.0 Ω) (0.5)
p.d. across 2.0 Ω = 2x2 = 4 V
p.d. across R₂ = 6 V (calculated before) (0.5)
Hence p.d. across R₁ = 12 − 6 − 4 = 2 V (0.5)
Current through R₁ = 2A (0.5)
Using Ohm’s Law, we get
R₁ = 2V/2A = 1Ω (0.5)
Alternative method
Total Resistance = R₁ + (4 x 12)/(4+12) + 2 = 12V/2 A = 6Ω (0.5)
R₁ = 6 – (3 + 2) = 1 Ω (0.5)

questions.text:
For visually impaired students
OR
B.
(i) State Joules law of heating and write its mathematical expression.
(ii) Two resistors of resistances 2Ω and 4Ω are connected in
a) series
b) parallel
with a battery of given potential difference. Compute the ratio of total quantity of heat produced in the combination in the two cases if the total voltage and time are kept the same for both.
questions.notes: Total 5 marks from Q36 scheme heading; this alternative has no explicit subpart mark breakdown. Source-verified against complete local text/coordinates and question crops; diagram-dependent and image-only formula evidence visually checked. Layout whitespace and mathematical glyphs normalized; wording/known source errors retained. Answer text is a source-faithful linear transcription; original layout is in answer evidence.
questions.answer:
B.
(i) Joule's Law of Heating states that the amount of heat produced in a conductor is directly proportional to the square of the electric current passing through it, the resistance of the conductor, and the time for which the current flows. Mathematically, it can be expressed as
H = I²Rt
H is the heat produced (in joules),
I is the electric current (in amperes),
R is the resistance of the conductor (in ohms),
t is the time for which the current flows (in seconds).
(ii) Let the equivalent resistance in series be denoted by R_s and that for parallel be denoted by R_p. Total voltage of the circuit is given by V in both cases and the time is denoted by t.
R_s = 2 + 4 = 6Ω

questions.answer:
(i) Maximum Resistance:
To get the maximum resistance, connect all four resistors in series.
The total resistance Rmax in series is the sum of the individual resistance:

(ii) Minimum Resistance:
To get the minimum resistance, connect all four resistors in parallel.

(i) Determine the cross-sectional area of the wire.

questions.answer:
(i) Show that the cross-sectional area of the wire is about 5 x 10⁻⁷ m².
The cross-sectional are A of a wire with diameter d is given by:
A = πd²/4
Substitute, d = 0.80 x 10⁻³ m:
A = π(0.80 × 10⁻³)²/4
A = π(0.64 × 10⁻⁶)/4
A = (2.01 × 10⁻⁶)/4 ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁷ m²
Thus, the cross-sectional are A is approximately 5 x 10⁻⁷ m².
(ii) To find the length l of the wire, we can use the formula of resistance:
R = ρl/A
Rearrange to solve for l:
l = RA/ρ
Substitute the values:
l = (0.12 × 5 × 10⁻⁷)/(1.8 × 10⁻⁸)
l = (6 × 10⁻⁸)/(1.8 × 10⁻⁸)
l = 6/1.8 ≈ 3.33 m
The student needs a length of approximately 3.33 m of given copper wire to make a 0.12 Ω resistor.

For visually impaired students
A.
(i) Explain why in household circuits only the fuse is connected in series with all the rest of the appliances but all appliances are connected in parallel to each other.
(ii) In a household circuit, an electric heater of power 1500 Wand a fan of power 500 W are connected in parallel to a 220 V supply. A fuse rated for 10 A is connected to the circuit to protect it from excessive current.
(a) Calculate the total current drawn by the heater and the fan.
(b) Determine whether the 10 A fuse is appropriate for this circuit or if it will blow.
questions.notes: Full alternative is included: fuse series placement and heating protection are explicitly NCERT Electricity section 11.7.1 (printed p190); appliance parallel connections are section 11.6. This overlaps domestic-circuit applications but requires no magnetic effects. Full printed total is 5; MS does not specify subpart allocations. Original source typos retained. questions.answer:
A.
(i) In household circuits, the fuse is connected in series with all appliances to ensure that it can cut off the entire circuit in case of excessive current, preventing hazards like fires or damage. This way, any overload or short circuit causes the fuse to blow, protecting all appliances.
Appliances are connected in parallel to ensure each receives the same voltage from the mains and can operate independently. This setup allows appliances to work simultaneously and efficiently, with each drawing only the current it needs, without affecting others.
Give Data:
Power of heater, Pheater = 1500 W
Power of Fan, Pfan = 500 W
Supply Voltage, V = 220 V
Fuse rating = 10 A
Step 1: Calculate the Current Drawn by Each Appliance
I = P/V
1. Current drawn by the heater: Iheater = 1500/220 = 6.82 A (rounded to two decimal places)
2. Current drawn by the fan: Ifan = Pfan/V = 500 W/220 V
Ifan = 2.27 A (rounded to two decimal places)
Step 2 : Calculate the total curent in the circuit
Since the heater and fan are connected in parallel, the total curent Itotal is the sum of the currents through each appliance:
Itotal = Iheater + Ifan = 6.82 + 2.27 = 9.09 A
Step 3: Compare with the Fuse Rating
The fuse is rated for 10 A, and the total current drawn by the heater and fan together is 9.09 A.
Since 9.09 A < 10 A, the fuse will not blow and is appropriate for this circuit, as the total current is within the fuse’s capacity.

questions.answer:
B.
Given data:
Resistor R₁ = 6 Ω
Resistor R₂ = 12 Ω
Voltage V = 24 V
Time t = 5 Minutes = 5 x 60 = 300 seconds
Step 1: Calculate the Current through each Resistor
Since the resistors are connected in parallel, the voltage across each resistor is the same as the battery voltage, V = 24 V.
Using Ohm’s Law,
Current through R₁: I₁ = V/R₁ = 24/6 = 4 A
Current through R₂: I₂ = V/R₂ = 24/12 = 2 A
Step 2: Calculate the Heat Generated in Each Resistor
Using Joule’s Law of Heating, H = I²Rt:
Heat generate in R₁: H₁ = 4² × 6 × 300 = 28800 J
Heat generate in R₂: H₂ = 2² × 12 × 300 = 14400 J
Total Heat Generated H: H = H₁ + H₂ = 28800 + 14400 = 43200 J
So, the total heat generated in both resistor is 43200 J.
Step 3 : Determine if each Resistor is safe
The power dissipated by each resistor can be calculated using P = V x I
Power dissipated by R₁: P₁ = 24 × 4 = 96 W
Power dissipated by R₂: P₂ = 24 × 2 = 48 W
Given that the power rating of each resistor is 100 W:
R₁ is operating at 96 W, which is within the 100 W limit. Hence, it is safe.
R₂ is operating at 48 W, which is also within the 100 W limit. Hence, it is safe.

questions.answer:
A.
I. Joule’s law of heating: The heat produced in a resistor is
(i) directly proportional to the square of current for a given resistance,
(ii) directly proportional to resistance for a given current, and
(iii) directly proportional to the time for which the current flows through the resistor.
H = I²Rt,
where ‘I’ is current and ‘R’ is resistance. (1)
II. If resistance is doubled: For the same current I, heat H becomes
H = I²(2R)t = 2I²Rt = 2H,
i.e. heat doubles. (1)

questions.exact_question_text:
As shown in the diagram, an electric circuit consisting of an ammeter, a voltmeter, 4 cells of 1·5 V each, a plug key with a gap XY was set up. Voltmeter and ammeter readings were recorded in the observation table for four arrangements as given below :
Arrangement No. 1 – only resistor R1 in gap XY
Arrangement No. 2 – only resistor R2 in gap XY
Arrangement No. 3 – Resistors R1 and R2 in series in gap XY
Arrangement No. 4 – Resistors R1 and R2 in parallel in gap XY
Based on the observations, four V – I graphs A, B, C and D as shown in figure were drawn. Study these graphs.
(a) Which one of the graphs represents the series combination of R1 and R2 ?
(b) Which one of these graphs represents the parallel combination of R1 and R2 ?
(c) (i) Show an arrangement of three resistors, each of resistance 10 Ω, so that the combination has a resistance of 15 Ω. Give justification for your answer.

[1 mark] (d) Charges circulate; electrical energy is transferred to the resistor, but charge is not consumed.

questions.text: 16. Constructed test data: a sealed box contains two positive resistors, each larger than zero, and no other components. (d) Identify which of these two arrangements fits, and explain why terminal data alone would not identify an arbitrary unknown network (1).

[1 mark] (c) Parallel gives 9 × 18/(9 + 18) = 6 Ω.
[1 mark] (d) Parallel fits the stated two choices. Other networks can also have 6 Ω equivalent resistance, so the inference relies on the stated components and choices.

Choose the shared assertion–reason option. [1 mark]

Correct option: A.
[1 mark] Both statements are true, and R explains A. Even if true I = V/R, adding a fixed meter offset shifts the plotted line away from the origin. The meter must be checked before blaming the resistor.

[1 mark] First interval: I1 = 9/30 = 0.30 A. Second: I2 = 9/10 = 0.90 A. Award 0.5 for each.

questions.text: A laboratory has two analogue ammeters: L has range 0–0.30 A with 30 equal divisions across its full scale; H has range 0–3.0 A with 30 equal divisions across its full scale. Both have negligible resistance, correct zero and no calibration error. Each is connected in series when used. For this task, a current change is considered resolvable only if it moves the pointer by at least one whole division; do not estimate fractions of a division. A chosen meter must also accommodate every expected current without exceeding full scale. (i) In the first test, current will stay between 0.18 A and 0.24 A, and changes of 0.02 A must be resolved. Choose L or H and justify the choice using both full scale and division size. [1 mark] (ii) In a second test, the current may reach 0.45 A, while the same 0.02 A changes must still be resolved. A student proposes switching to H. Does either available meter now meet both requirements? Justify your decision and state the full-scale and division-size requirements for a suitable replacement. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] Choose L. Its division size is 0.30/30 = 0.010 A, so a 0.02 A change spans two divisions, and the largest expected current, 0.24 A, is below its 0.30 A full scale. H can accommodate the current but has 3.0/30 = 0.10 A per division; a 0.02 A change spans only 0.2 division and fails the stated resolution rule. Award the mark for the choice justified against both range and resolution, not division-size arithmetic alone.
[1 mark] Neither meter meets both requirements in the second test. L would be over range because 0.45 A exceeds 0.30 A. H has enough range but still cannot resolve a 0.02 A change under the one-whole-division rule. Use a replacement with full scale at least 0.45 A and division size no greater than 0.02 A; for example, a 0–0.60 A meter with 60 equal divisions has 0.010 A per division and satisfies both. Award the mark for rejecting both available meters on the correct grounds and specifying both replacement requirements.

Arithmetic supports these decisions and earns no stand-alone mark. No wire-control rehearsal or zero-offset correction is required.

questions.text: A uniform wire has length 0.50 m, cross-sectional area 0.20 mm² and measured resistance 2.0 Ω at a fixed temperature. (i) Calculate its resistivity in SI units. [1 mark] (ii) The wire is cut into two equal lengths without stretching. A student says each half has half the resistivity. Correct the claim and state each half’s resistance. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] A = 0.20 × 10⁻⁶ m² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ m². ρ = RA/L = 2.0 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁷/0.50 = 8.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.
[1 mark] Each half has resistance 1.0 Ω because length halves while area is unchanged. Resistivity stays 8.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m because material and temperature have not changed.

marking_scheme.step: Each half has resistance 1.0 Ω because length halves while area is unchanged. Resistivity stays 8.0 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m because material and temperature have not changed.

questions.competency_rationale: Only (ii), distinguishing material property from specimen resistance, earns competency credit.

questions.text: A 2 Ω and a 5 Ω resistor are in series across an ideal 7 V source. An accurate ammeter in the single loop reads 1 A. A voltmeter placed in turn across each resistor reports 3 V and 6 V. All resistances and temperature remain constant. (i) Show why the two voltage readings cannot both be correct. [1 mark] (ii) If the voltmeter has one constant added offset and no other error, determine it and state the corrected readings. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] The drops should add to 7 V, but 3 + 6 = 9 V. Independently, IR predicts 2 V and 5 V at 1 A.
[1 mark] Each reading is 1 V too high: 3 − 2 = 6 − 5 = 1 V. The offset is +1 V; subtract 1 V to obtain 2 V and 5 V. The total excess of 2 V is shared over two readings.

questions.text: Two unlabelled resistors are connected in parallel across an ideal 6 V source. Accurate ammeters show 0.75 A from the source and 0.25 A in one branch. (i) Infer the current in the other branch and explain the inference. [1 mark] (ii) A label claiming that the other branch resistor is 24 Ω is proposed. Accept or reject it quantitatively. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] Other branch current = 0.75 − 0.25 = 0.50 A, since the source current equals the sum of the steady branch currents.
[1 mark] Reject: both branches have 6 V across them; the other branch resistance is 6/0.50 = 12 Ω, not 24 Ω. A 24 Ω branch would carry only 0.25 A.

questions.answer:
[1 mark] At 2 V, I = 0.20 A and V/I = 10 Ω. At 6 V, I = 0.40 A and V/I = 15 Ω. Award 0.5 for each correctly read and calculated pair.

questions.text: The supplied circuit is a proposed resistance-measurement setup. The switch is closed, the 5 V source is ideal, meter M is an ideal voltmeter, and meter N is an ideal ammeter. The resistor is 10 Ω. (i) Explain why M is incorrectly placed and predict the circuit current. [1 mark] (ii) Explain why N is incorrectly placed; also explain why N does not cause an unbounded source current in this particular faulty setup. [1 mark] (iii) State the rewiring needed for a valid measurement and give the two corrected readings. Disconnect the source before rewiring. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] M is in the only source path. An ideal voltmeter draws no current, so it behaves as an open path in series and the source current is zero.
[1 mark] N is across the 10 Ω resistor; its zero resistance bypasses the resistor. Nevertheless M already breaks the source path, so no complete zero-resistance path spans the source and no unbounded source current occurs.
[1 mark] Put N in series with the resistor and M across the resistor endpoints X and Y. With the ideal 5 V source the readings are IN = 5/10 = 0.50 A and VM = 5 V. The corrected ammeter must not remain across X and Y.

questions.text: A 6 Ω and a 12 Ω resistor are joined in parallel across an ideal 6 V source. The 12 Ω branch is then disconnected, leaving the 6 Ω branch intact. (i) Calculate the initial equivalent resistance. [1 mark] (ii) Predict the change in total source current and explain why it changes. [1 mark] (iii) A student says the remaining branch now receives the old total current. Test that claim with its new current and voltage. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] 1/Req = 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4, so Req = 4 Ω.
[1 mark] Initially the source current is 6/4 = 1.5 A. After removal it is 6/6 = 1.0 A; the lost branch no longer contributes its 0.5 A.
[1 mark] The remaining branch still has 6 V and 6 Ω, so its current remains 1.0 A, not 1.5 A. An ideal voltage source does not maintain the old total current.

questions.text: A team compares electrical heat generated in two identical constant-resistance coils. Trial A uses 0.40 A for 150 s. Trial B uses 0.60 A for 100 s. No heat escapes the collecting system, and the heat generated equals the measured collected energy. (i) Without needing the coil resistance, find HB/HA. [1 mark] (ii) A student argues that the heat must be equal because the same charge passed. Evaluate this argument, including the charge values. [1 mark] (iii) Find the duration at 0.60 A that would generate the same heat as trial A. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Charge versus heat in controlled trials
questions.answer:
[1 mark] HB/HA = (0.60² × 100)/(0.40² × 150) = 36/24 = 1.5; the common resistance cancels.
[1 mark] Both charges are 60 C: 0.40 × 150 = 0.60 × 100. But heat is not fixed by charge alone. At higher current the same coil has higher voltage, so each coulomb transfers more energy; trial B generates 1.5 times as much heat.
[1 mark] Equate I²Rt: tB = 0.40² × 150/0.60² = 66.7 s approximately. Use the same resistance in both trials.

questions.text: A resistive test lamp is labelled 12 V, 6 W. Its resistance is assumed constant at the rated value. (i) Determine that resistance. [1 mark] (ii) A technician proposes a 6 V source, arguing that the lamp will then use 3 W because the voltage is halved. Test the claim and state the actual power. [1 mark] (iii) Can your result alone predict the exact perceived brightness of a real filament lamp whose resistance changes with temperature? Explain. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] R = V²/P = 12²/6 = 24 Ω.
[1 mark] The claim is false under the constant-R assumption. Pnew = 6²/24 = 1.5 W, one-quarter of 6 W, because power varies as V² at fixed R.
[1 mark] No. A real filament’s changing temperature changes its resistance, and perceived brightness is not specified by this constant-resistance electrical model. The 1.5 W result applies to the given model, not an exact brightness prediction.

[1 mark] (ii) Is the recorded total consistent with the operating times? Support your conclusion with the expected value. [1 mark] (iii) The recorder counted the heater as on for the full session. Show whether this timing error explains the recorded total exactly; do not assume an electrical fault. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] Lamp: 0.040 × 1.5 = 0.060 kWh. Heater: 0.200 × 0.30 = 0.060 kWh. Total = 0.120 kWh.
[1 mark] No: 0.36 kWh is three times the expected 0.12 kWh, an excess of 0.24 kWh, for the actual stated operation.
[1 mark] Using 1.5 h incorrectly for the heater gives 0.200 × 1.5 + 0.060 = 0.360 kWh, matching the recorded total exactly. The accounting error explains the number without requiring any electrical fault.

questions.text: Two sealed boxes each contain a single uniform wire. At the same controlled temperature, both have measured resistance 8 Ω. Box X contains a wire of length L and area A. Box Y contains one of length 2L and area 3A. (i) Derive ρY/ρX from these measurements. [1 mark] (ii) A student identifies both wires as the same material solely because their resistances agree. Is the identification supported? [1 mark] (iii) Suggest a different geometry for a new sample of material Y that would allow a direct resistance comparison with X to compare resistivities. [1 mark]

[1 mark] ρ = RA/L, so ρY/ρX = (8 × 3A/(2L))/(8 × A/L) = 3/2.

Also accept any new geometry with the same length-to-area ratio L/A, such as length 2L and area 2A, with the same temperature. Matching only one dimension while leaving the other unequal is insufficient.

questions.text: A laboratory ammeter is checked using one ohmic resistor kept at constant temperature. The applied voltage is measured accurately, including a no-current check at 0 V. The supplied graph contains the observations. The ammeter has negligible resistance and its only possible fault is a constant added current indication. (i) Read the no-current indication and state the correction to every reading. [1 mark] (ii) Use the change between the plotted 2 V and 6 V observations to determine the resistor’s resistance. Explain in ordinary words why subtracting the two indications removes a constant offset. Do not use statistical fitting. [2 marks] (iii) A student divides 2 V by the indicated current at 2 V and reports the result as the resistance. Calculate that result and explain the discrepancy. [1 mark] (iv) Predict the ammeter indication at an accurately applied 3 V after leaving the offset unadjusted. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Offset meter calibration from a graph
questions.answer:

[1 mark] The uncorrected result is 2/0.30 = 6.67 Ω approximately, too small. The numerator is correct but the denominator includes 0.10 A that is not actual current; a ratio from the origin is inappropriate for the shifted line.
[1 mark] True current at 3 V is 3/10 = 0.30 A. The unadjusted meter adds 0.10 A, so it indicates 0.40 A.

questions.text: A team is given the three uniform cylindrical wire specimens in the supplied diagram. All are made from the same alloy and are held at the same temperature; L and d are positive. Each specimen is tested separately at an accurately measured 1.2 V, using ideal meters and negligible-resistance leads. (i) Select the pair that isolates the effect of length, and justify your choice from the figure. [1 mark] (ii) Select the pair that isolates the effect of diameter, and state the ratio of their cross-sectional areas. [1 mark] (iii) The current for P is 0.12 A. Predict the currents for Q and R, using the displayed geometries. [2 marks] (iv) A team instead compares only P with Q and concludes that doubling length halves resistance. Explain why this is not a valid length-only conclusion even if its measured resistance ratio is correct. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] Q and R isolate length: they have the same alloy, temperature and diameter 2d, while Q has length 2L and R has length L.
[1 mark] P and R isolate diameter: both have length L, the same material and temperature. Diameters are d and 2d, so AR/AP = (2d/d)² = 4, not 2.
[1 mark] For P, RP = 1.2/0.12 = 10 Ω. Q has twice the length and four times the area of P, so RQ/RP = 2/4 = 1/2. RQ = 5 Ω and IQ = 1.2/5 = 0.24 A.
[1 mark] R has the same length and four times the area of P, so RR = RP/4 = 2.5 Ω. IR = 1.2/2.5 = 0.48 A.
[1 mark] P and Q differ in diameter as well as length. The area increase outweighs the length increase. With area held constant, doubling length doubles resistance; the halved resistance in this pair is a combined-geometry effect, not the isolated length effect.

marking_scheme.step: Q and R isolate length: they have the same alloy, temperature and diameter 2d, while Q has length 2L and R has length L.
P and R isolate diameter: both have length L, the same material and temperature. Diameters are d and 2d, so AR/AP = (2d/d)² = 4, not 2.
For P, RP = 1.2/0.12 = 10 Ω. Q has twice the length and four times the area of P, so RQ/RP = 2/4 = 1/2. RQ = 5 Ω and IQ = 1.2/5 = 0.24 A.
R has the same length and four times the area of P, so RR = RP/4 = 2.5 Ω. IR = 1.2/2.5 = 0.48 A.

P and Q differ in diameter as well as length. The area increase outweighs the length increase. With area held constant, doubling length doubles resistance; the halved resistance in this pair is a combined-geometry effect, not the isolated length effect.

questions.competency_rationale: Controlled-pair selection in (i)–(ii) and the confounding critique in (iv) earn three marks. The two numerical current predictions in (iii) are excluded conservatively.
