questions.text: A technician is checking a 10 Ω standard resistor using an ideal 6 V source and accurate, ideal meters. The ammeter is in the single series path; the voltmeter is connected directly to the standard resistor’s own terminals. The source terminal voltage is confirmed as 6 V, but the readings are I = 0.40 A and Vresistor = 4.0 V. Exactly one fault is present: either (A) the standard resistor has changed resistance, or (B) one contact elsewhere in the series path has acquired resistance. All other leads and contacts have zero resistance. (i) Use the two meter readings to decide whether the standard itself is still 10 Ω. [1 mark] (ii) Choose A or B and determine the faulty contact resistance. [2 marks] (iii) Specify a voltage measurement that would confirm the location of the fault without moving the ammeter, and predict its reading. [1 mark] (iv) Calculate the electrical power generated as heat in the faulty contact. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] The standard’s measured resistance is Vresistor/I = 4.0/0.40 = 10 Ω. It has not changed under the stated alternatives.
[1 mark] Choose B. The contact must account for the source voltage not appearing across the standard: Vcontact = 6 − 4 = 2 V.
[1 mark] The same 0.40 A flows through the contact, so Rcontact = 2/0.40 = 5 Ω. Check: total resistance 15 Ω gives 6/15 = 0.40 A.
[1 mark] Place the ideal voltmeter across the two sides of the suspect contact, keeping the series ammeter in place. The faulty contact reads 2 V; a sound zero-resistance contact reads 0 V. Probe contacts in turn if its position is not yet known.
[1 mark] Pcontact = I²Rcontact = 0.40² × 5 = 0.80 W, also 2 V × 0.40 A. This is electrical heat generation, not a temperature-rise prediction.

marking_scheme.step: The standard’s measured resistance is Vresistor/I = 4.0/0.40 = 10 Ω. It has not changed under the stated alternatives.
Choose B. The contact must account for the source voltage not appearing across the standard: Vcontact = 6 − 4 = 2 V.
The same 0.40 A flows through the contact, so Rcontact = 2/0.40 = 5 Ω. Check: total resistance 15 Ω gives 6/15 = 0.40 A.

Place the ideal voltmeter across the two sides of the suspect contact, keeping the series ammeter in place. The faulty contact reads 2 V; a sound zero-resistance contact reads 0 V. Probe contacts in turn if its position is not yet known.
Pcontact = I²Rcontact = 0.40² × 5 = 0.80 W, also 2 V × 0.40 A. This is electrical heat generation, not a temperature-rise prediction.

questions.competency_rationale: Count the unchanged-standard diagnosis in (i), selection of fault B using the missing voltage in (ii), and confirmatory probe design in (iii). Exclude the one-mark contact-resistance substitution within (ii) and the final power substitution.

questions.text: A charge counter records cumulative charge crossing a section of a test circuit. Its readings form the supplied piecewise straight graph; segments represent constant current, not instantaneous jumps in charge. The counter is in the source lead and records all charge delivered by an ideal 3 V source. A switch selects different fixed resistive loads for the two rising intervals and opens the circuit during the horizontal interval. Ignore switching transients; each selected load has constant resistance. (i) Identify the interval in which the circuit carries no current and justify this from the graph. [1 mark] (ii) Determine the currents in the first and final rising intervals, using changes in charge and time. [1 mark] (iii) A student claims that the equal charge increments in those two intervals require equal power. Test the claim by comparing their electrical powers and total energies. [2 marks]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] No current flows from 20 s to 40 s because cumulative charge stays at 8 C; no additional charge crosses the section.
[1 mark] First rising interval: I = (8 − 0)/(20 − 0) = 0.40 A. Final rising interval: I = (16 − 8)/(50 − 40) = 0.80 A. Award 0.5 for each.
[1 mark] The claim is false: Pfirst = 3 × 0.40 = 1.2 W and Plast = 3 × 0.80 = 2.4 W. Equal charge was transferred in different durations, so powers differ.
[1 mark] The total energy in each rising interval is nevertheless equal: E = VΔQ = 3 × 8 = 24 J. Checks: 1.2 × 20 = 2.4 × 10 = 24 J. Equal energy is not equal power.

marking_scheme.step: No current flows from 20 s to 40 s because cumulative charge stays at 8 C; no additional charge crosses the section.
First rising interval: I = (8 − 0)/(20 − 0) = 0.40 A. Final rising interval: I = (16 − 8)/(50 − 40) = 0.80 A. Award 0.5 for each.
The claim is false: Pfirst = 3 × 0.40 = 1.2 W and Plast = 3 × 0.80 = 2.4 W. Equal charge was transferred in different durations, so powers differ.
The total energy in each rising interval is nevertheless equal: E = VΔQ = 3 × 8 = 24 J. Checks: 1.2 × 20 = 2.4 × 10 = 24 J. Equal energy is not equal power.

questions.competency_rationale: Only the two marks in (iii), distinguishing equal energy from unequal power using the two intervals, are counted. Zero-current interval reading and direct current calculations in (i)–(ii) are foundational.

diagram_image.alt: Cumulative charge versus elapsed time with three straight segments.

questions.text: A lab group records the following accurate observations for two constant-resistance components, keeping each at the same temperature throughout: X alone: 3 V, 0.30 A; Y alone: 3 V, 0.15 A. The components are then put inside a sealed box using either series or parallel connection, with no other components and with zero-resistance connecting leads. The resistors dissipate electrical energy as heat. Across the box the group measures 6 V and 0.20 A. (i) Find RX and RY from the individual observations. [1 mark] (ii) Identify the connection inside the box using the box measurements. [1 mark] (iii) Another group claims the box could be parallel if the current merely divided equally. Test that alternative by calculating its total current at 6 V and explaining why equal division is not valid here. [2 marks]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] RX = 3/0.30 = 10 Ω and RY = 3/0.15 = 20 Ω. Award 0.5 for each.
[1 mark] Rbox = 6/0.20 = 30 Ω, which equals 10 + 20. The box is series, under the two allowed alternatives.
[1 mark] For parallel at 6 V, IX = 6/10 = 0.60 A and IY = 6/20 = 0.30 A; total = 0.90 A, not the measured 0.20 A.
[1 mark] Parallel branches have equal voltage, not necessarily equal current. Unequal resistances give unequal branch currents (here in ratio 2:1), so equal splitting cannot rescue the proposed parallel explanation.

marking_scheme.step: RX = 3/0.30 = 10 Ω and RY = 3/0.15 = 20 Ω. Award 0.5 for each.
Rbox = 6/0.20 = 30 Ω, which equals 10 + 20. The box is series, under the two allowed alternatives.
For parallel at 6 V, IX = 6/10 = 0.60 A and IY = 6/20 = 0.30 A; total = 0.90 A, not the measured 0.20 A.

Parallel branches have equal voltage, not necessarily equal current. Unequal resistances give unequal branch currents (here in ratio 2:1), so equal splitting cannot rescue the proposed parallel explanation.

questions.competency_rationale: The isolated resistance calculations are foundational. Connection inference and testing the rival branch model earn the other three marks.

questions.text: A heating experiment uses a constant-resistance coil at an accurately maintained 5 V and 0.40 A for 120 s. A heat collector captures only the energy reaching it from the coil; it reports 180 J. Any remaining electrical energy is transferred as heat to the surroundings, and there is no other energy input. A student writes: “The coil resistance must be wrong because the collector should read all the electrical energy.” (i) Find the electrical energy supplied and the energy not captured by the collector. [1 mark] (ii) Does the collector reading alone support the student’s diagnosis? Use the electrical readings and the stated energy pathway. [1 mark] (iii) In a repeat, voltage, current and duration are unchanged but improved insulation gives a collector reading of 225 J. Decide whether the coil generated more electrical heat, and quantify what changed. [2 marks]
questions.answer:
[1 mark] Electrical energy E = VIt = 5 × 0.40 × 120 = 240 J. Energy not captured = 240 − 180 = 60 J. Award 0.5 for each.
[1 mark] No. The electrical readings give R = V/I = 12.5 Ω. The collector measures only the captured portion, not all generated heat. The 60 J transferred to the surroundings is an allowed explanation; lower collection does not diagnose wrong resistance.
[1 mark] Electrical heat generated stays 240 J because V, I and t are unchanged. Better insulation does not change that electrical input under the stated conditions.
[1 mark] The captured energy increases by 225 − 180 = 45 J. Heat going to the surroundings falls from 60 J to 240 − 225 = 15 J, a decrease of 45 J. This is redistribution of the same generated heat, not additional generation.

marking_scheme.step: Electrical energy E = VIt = 5 × 0.40 × 120 = 240 J. Energy not captured = 240 − 180 = 60 J. Award 0.5 for each.

No. The electrical readings give R = V/I = 12.5 Ω. The collector measures only the captured portion, not all generated heat. The 60 J transferred to the surroundings is an allowed explanation; lower collection does not diagnose wrong resistance.
Electrical heat generated stays 240 J because V, I and t are unchanged. Better insulation does not change that electrical input under the stated conditions.

The captured energy increases by 225 − 180 = 45 J. Heat going to the surroundings falls from 60 J to 240 − 225 = 15 J, a decrease of 45 J. This is redistribution of the same generated heat, not additional generation.

questions.competency_rationale: Count (ii), rejecting resistance diagnosis from incomplete heat collection, and the first mark of (iii), unchanged generated heat under a controlled repeat. Exclude initial energy arithmetic and the final one-mark collected/lost-energy subtraction.

questions.text: In a metal wire in a closed circuit, conventional current is directed from point P towards point Q. In which direction is the net drift of electrons? [1 mark]
options: From P towards Q, in the direction of conventional current
From Q towards P, opposite to conventional current
There is no net electron drift when current flows
Electrons drift equally in both directions, giving zero net drift
questions.answer: B. Electrons carry negative charge. Their net drift is opposite to the defined direction of conventional current, so they drift from Q towards P. Random electron motion does not remove this net drift. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose B. Electrons carry negative charge. Their net drift is opposite to the defined direction of conventional current, so they drift from Q towards P. Random electron motion does not remove this net drift.

questions.competency_rationale: Foundational recall of the opposite directions of conventional current and electron drift; zero competency marks.

questions.text: An ideal source maintaining a nonzero constant voltage is connected to a resistor and a switch in series. An ideal voltmeter remains connected directly across the source terminals. What happens to its reading when the switch changes from open to closed? [1 mark]
options: It is zero with the switch open and nonzero when closed.
It is nonzero with the switch open and zero when closed.
It has the same nonzero value in both switch positions.
It doubles when the switch is closed.
questions.answer: C. The ideal source maintains its terminal potential difference even when the resistor path is open and no current flows through that path. Closing the switch permits current through the resistor but does not change the ideal source voltage, so the voltmeter reading remains the same. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose C. The ideal source maintains its terminal potential difference even when the resistor path is open and no current flows through that path. Closing the switch permits current through the resistor but does not change the ideal source voltage, so the voltmeter reading remains the same.

questions.competency_rationale: Foundational distinction between source potential difference and a closed conducting path; no numerical substitution and zero competency marks.

questions.text: In 30 s, 90 C enters a junction feeding two branches. One branch carries a steady 0.80 A. There is no charge accumulation. What current flows in the other branch? [1 mark]
questions.answer: A. The incoming current is 90/30 = 3 A. Branch currents add, so the other current is 3 − 0.80 = 2.20 A. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose A. The incoming current is 90/30 = 3 A. Branch currents add, so the other current is 3 − 0.80 = 2.20 A.

questions.competency_rationale: Conservative audit: routine current conversion followed by subtraction; no separate competency credit.

questions.text: In the supplied figure, the link K is an ideal conducting wire, not an open switch. What are the source current and the current through the 6 Ω resistor, respectively? [1 mark]
questions.answer: D. K joins both ends of the 6 Ω resistor with negligible resistance, making its voltage and current zero. Only 3 Ω limits the source current: 9/3 = 3 A. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose D. K joins both ends of the 6 Ω resistor with negligible resistance, making its voltage and current zero. Only 3 Ω limits the source current: 9/3 = 3 A.

questions.competency_rationale: The wire topology must be interpreted before any resistance calculation; the bypass is not a third resistive branch.

diagram_image.alt: Question 4: original bypass figure; labels and connections are part of the question.

questions.text: A 10 Ω resistor is alone across an ideal 5 V source. A 15 Ω resistor is then added in parallel. Which statement correctly describes the original resistor? [1 mark]
options: Its current falls because current is shared equally.
Its current stays 0.50 A while source current increases.
Its current becomes the total source current.
questions.answer: B. Its voltage remains 5 V and its current remains 5/10 = 0.50 A; the source additionally supplies 5/15 A to the new branch. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose B. Its voltage remains 5 V and its current remains 5/10 = 0.50 A; the source additionally supplies 5/15 A to the new branch.

questions.competency_rationale: Distinguish unchanged branch voltage from changed total source current.

questions.text: At a specified temperature, which pair correctly identifies a material property and a property of a particular uniform wire specimen, respectively? [1 mark]
options: Resistance of the wire; resistivity of its material
Length of the wire; resistivity of its material
Resistivity of the material; resistance of the wire
Cross-sectional area of the wire; length of the wire
questions.answer: C. Resistivity characterises the material at a specified temperature. The resistance of a particular wire also depends on its length and cross-sectional area through R = ρL/A. Length and area describe specimens, not intrinsic material properties. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose C. Resistivity characterises the material at a specified temperature. The resistance of a particular wire also depends on its length and cross-sectional area through R = ρL/A. Length and area describe specimens, not intrinsic material properties.

questions.competency_rationale: Foundational classification of resistivity versus resistance and dimensions; zero competency marks.

questions.text: A replacement cylindrical wire has twice the length and half the diameter of the original. Material and temperature are unchanged. Its resistance is what multiple of the original resistance? [1 mark]
questions.answer: A. Area becomes one-quarter; R ∝ L/A gives Rnew/Rold = 2/(1/4) = 8. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose A. Area becomes one-quarter; R ∝ L/A gives Rnew/Rold = 2/(1/4) = 8.

questions.competency_rationale: Account for the squared diameter dependence while combining two geometry changes.

questions.text: The figure gives the separate I–V traces of two ohmic resistors X and Y at constant temperature; I is vertical and V is horizontal. Both resistors are then used once, either in series or in parallel, across an adjustable ideal source. A proposed trace for the combined network is a straight line through the origin and the point (V = 3.0 V, I = 0.90 A), where I is the total source current. Which conclusion correctly tests the proposed trace against the figure? [1 mark]
questions.topic: Graph evidence for a proposed network trace
options: The series connection fits: at 3.0 V the total current is 0.90 A.
The series connection fits: at 3.0 V the total current is 0.60 A.
The parallel connection fits: at 3.0 V the total current is 0.20 A.
The parallel connection fits: at 3.0 V the total current is 0.90 A.
questions.answer: D. Read the separate traces at 3.0 V: IX = 0.60 A and IY = 0.30 A. In parallel both resistors have this voltage, so total current is 0.60 + 0.30 = 0.90 A and the proposed trace fits. For series, RX = 3.0/0.60 = 5 Ω and RY = 3.0/0.30 = 10 Ω; total current would be 3.0/(5 + 10) = 0.20 A, not 0.90 A. At constant resistance both network traces are straight through the origin. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose D. Read the separate traces at 3.0 V: IX = 0.60 A and IY = 0.30 A. In parallel both resistors have this voltage, so total current is 0.60 + 0.30 = 0.90 A and the proposed trace fits. For series, RX = 3.0/0.60 = 5 Ω and RY = 3.0/0.30 = 10 Ω; total current would be 3.0/(5 + 10) = 0.20 A, not 0.90 A. At constant resistance both network traces are straight through the origin.

questions.competency_rationale: One competency mark for extracting two currents from the supplied graph and testing competing series/parallel connection models against a proposed total-current trace; not a material-ratio inference or an isolated supplied-value substitution.

diagram_image.alt: Question 8: separate current–voltage traces labelled X and Y; read the axes and line values from the figure.

questions.text: Resistors 4 Ω and 8 Ω are in series. An ideal voltmeter reads 4 V across the 4 Ω resistor. Without changing the circuit, it is moved to span both resistors. What will it read? [1 mark]
questions.answer: C. The shared current is 4/4 = 1 A. Across 4 + 8 = 12 Ω the reading is 1 × 12 = 12 V. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose C. The shared current is 4/4 = 1 A. Across 4 + 8 = 12 Ω the reading is 1 × 12 = 12 V.

questions.competency_rationale: Conservative audit: standard series-current and total-voltage calculation; changing voltmeter endpoints alone is insufficient for competency credit.

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes one kilowatt-hour? [1 mark]
options: A power of 1000 W per hour
A current of 1000 A in one hour
questions.answer: B. It is energy used at 1000 W for 3600 s, equal to 3.6 × 10⁶ J; it is not a power. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose B. It is energy used at 1000 W for 3600 s, equal to 3.6 × 10⁶ J; it is not a power.

questions.competency_rationale: Foundational meaning and conversion of an energy unit.

questions.text: A resistor R is replaced by a resistor 2R across the same ideal voltage source for the same time. What happens to the heat generated? [1 mark]
questions.answer: A. H = V²t/R at fixed voltage and time, so doubling R halves H. The current is not fixed. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose A. H = V²t/R at fixed voltage and time, so doubling R halves H. The current is not fixed.

questions.competency_rationale: Conservative audit: direct inverse proportionality at stated fixed voltage and time; foundational.

questions.text: Three separate resistors are connected in parallel directly across an ideal source. One develops a complete break internally. What happens to the other two steady branch currents? [1 mark]
options: They become equal regardless of resistance.
questions.answer: D. The two intact branches remain across the same source voltage with unchanged resistance, so their currents remain unchanged; only source current falls. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose D. The two intact branches remain across the same source voltage with unchanged resistance, so their currents remain unchanged; only source current falls.

questions.competency_rationale: Conservative audit: direct recall of ideal parallel-branch independence; foundational despite fault wording.

questions.text: A 2 Ω resistor rated at a maximum 2 W and an 8 Ω resistor rated at a maximum 8 W are in series. Ratings may be reached but not exceeded. Which is the largest source voltage that is allowed for both? [1 mark]
questions.answer: C. Each permits at most 1 A: √(2/2) = √(8/8) = 1. Thus Vmax = 1 × (2 + 8) = 10 V. At 12 V both ratings would be exceeded. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose C. Each permits at most 1 A: √(2/2) = √(8/8) = 1. Thus Vmax = 1 × (2 + 8) = 10 V. At 12 V both ratings would be exceeded.

questions.competency_rationale: Find the limiting current for each component rather than summing ratings without checking distribution.

questions.text: A device consumes a constant 50 W for 2 h. How much electrical energy does it consume? [1 mark]
questions.answer: B. E = Pt = 0.050 kW × 2 h = 0.10 kWh. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose B. E = Pt = 0.050 kW × 2 h = 0.10 kWh.

questions.competency_rationale: Single power-time substitution and unit conversion.

questions.text: In a wire experiment the measured voltage remains 6.0 V, but the current falls from 0.60 A immediately after connection to 0.50 A later. Which conclusion is supported by these readings alone? [1 mark]
options: The charge of each electron increased.
The readings prove the wire became colder.
questions.answer: A. V/I increases from 10 Ω to 12 Ω. The readings establish increased resistance but do not alone prove heating is the cause; temperature should be monitored or controlled. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose A. V/I increases from 10 Ω to 12 Ω. The readings establish increased resistance but do not alone prove heating is the cause; temperature should be monitored or controlled.

questions.competency_rationale: Distinguish a measured resistance change from an unproved explanation of its cause.

questions.text: Two model lamps rated 12 V, 6 W and 12 V, 12 W are connected in series across 12 V. Treat their resistances as constant at their rated values and brightness as proportional to electrical power. Which is brighter? [1 mark]
options: The 12 W lamp, because its rated power is higher.
They are equally bright because their current is equal.
The 6 W lamp, because its resistance is greater.
questions.answer: D. Their resistances are 24 Ω and 12 Ω. In series both carry the same current, so I²R is larger in the 24 Ω lamp: the lamp rated 6 W is brighter in this connection. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose D. Their resistances are 24 Ω and 12 Ω. In series both carry the same current, so I²R is larger in the 24 Ω lamp: the lamp rated 6 W is brighter in this connection.

questions.competency_rationale: Convert ratings to resistances and then compare powers under the new common-current condition.

questions.text: Assertion (A): In a steady series circuit, the current before and after a resistor is the same. Reason (R): A series circuit has no branch path and charge does not accumulate in the resistor. [1 mark]
options: both true and R correctly explains A
both true but R does not correctly explain A
questions.answer: A. A and R are true. With no branching or accumulation, the same charge per second must enter and leave, so R explains A. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose A. A and R are true. With no branching or accumulation, the same charge per second must enter and leave, so R explains A.

questions.competency_rationale: Direct chapter principle and its standard explanation; conservatively foundational.

questions.text: Assertion (A): Cutting a uniform wire into two equal lengths halves the resistivity of each piece at the same temperature. Reason (R): Resistivity is a characteristic of the material at a specified temperature. [1 mark]
options: both true and R correctly explains A
both true but R does not correctly explain A
questions.answer: D. A is false: each piece has half the resistance, but unchanged resistivity. R is true. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose D. A is false: each piece has half the resistance, but unchanged resistivity. R is true.

questions.competency_rationale: Conservative audit: textbook distinction between resistance and resistivity; foundational A/R item.

questions.text: Assertion (A): Two unequal resistors connected in parallel have the same potential difference. Reason (R): One volt equals one joule per coulomb. [1 mark]
options: both true and R correctly explains A
both true but R does not correctly explain A
questions.answer: B. Both are true, but the unit definition does not explain voltage equality. Equality follows because both resistors join the same two nodes. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose B. Both are true, but the unit definition does not explain voltage equality. Equality follows because both resistors join the same two nodes.

questions.competency_rationale: Recognize two textbook facts and an explanatory mismatch; no conservative competency credit.

questions.text: Assertion (A): Doubling a resistor’s resistance while keeping its voltage fixed doubles its power. Reason (R): For a resistor, P = V²/R. [1 mark]
options: both true and R correctly explains A
both true but R does not correctly explain A
questions.answer: D. A is false: doubling R at fixed V halves P. R is true and gives that result directly. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Choose D. A is false: doubling R at fixed V halves P. R is true and gives that result directly.

questions.competency_rationale: Conservative audit: the supplied reason gives the formula and assertion needs only direct inverse proportionality; foundational.

questions.text: During the same 40 s interval, 64 C passes through the supply lead of a two-branch circuit and 24 C passes through branch X. A student says branch Y must carry the same current as X because both are parallel. (i) Determine the current in Y. (1 mark) (ii) Decide whether the student’s claim is valid, explaining the governing relationship. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. No charge accumulates, so QY = 64 − 24 = 40 C. IY = QY/t = 40/40 = 1.0 A. [1 mark]
2. IX = 24/40 = 0.60 A, not 1.0 A. In parallel the voltages are equal, while branch currents depend on resistance and add to the 1.60 A supply current. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: No charge accumulates, so QY = 64 − 24 = 40 C. IY = QY/t = 40/40 = 1.0 A.
IX = 24/40 = 0.60 A, not 1.0 A. In parallel the voltages are equal, while branch currents depend on resistance and add to the 1.60 A supply current.

questions.competency_rationale: Infer missing branch flow from simultaneous charge records and refute equality of parallel currents.

questions.text: A charge of 15 C passes through a resistor across which the potential difference is 8 V. (i) State what a potential difference of 8 V means in terms of energy and charge. (1 mark) (ii) Calculate the electrical energy transferred to the resistor. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. A potential difference of 8 V means 8 J of energy is transferred per coulomb passing between the resistor’s terminals. [1 mark]
2. W = VQ = 8 × 15 = 120 J. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: A potential difference of 8 V means 8 J of energy is transferred per coulomb passing between the resistor’s terminals.

questions.competency_rationale: Definition and direct calculation; neither subpart is counted as competency.

questions.text: A current meter consistently displays +0.04 A with no current. It then displays 0.34 A while an ideal voltmeter reads 3.6 V across a resistor. Apart from this additive zero offset, the current meter is ideal. A report gives the resistance as 3.6/0.34 ≈ 10.6 Ω. (i) Find the corrected resistance. (1 mark) (ii) Explain whether the reported value is too high or too low, without merely quoting your result. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. Subtract the positive zero offset: I = 0.34 − 0.04 = 0.30 A. R = 3.6/0.30 = 12 Ω. [1 mark]
2. The uncorrected current is too large. Dividing the same voltage by too large a current gives too small a resistance, so 10.6 Ω is an underestimate. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Subtract the positive zero offset: I = 0.34 − 0.04 = 0.30 A. R = 3.6/0.30 = 12 Ω.
The uncorrected current is too large. Dividing the same voltage by too large a current gives too small a resistance, so 10.6 Ω is an underestimate.

questions.competency_rationale: Correct systematic error and determine the direction of its effect on an inferred resistance.

questions.text: A student tests whether wire resistance depends on length by comparing a short thin copper wire with a long thick alloy wire at the same voltage. (i) Explain why this test cannot isolate the effect of length. (1 mark) (ii) Specify a corrected pair of wires and one operating precaution needed for the comparison. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. Length, cross-sectional area and material all differ. A current/resistance difference could be due to any of them, so length has not been isolated. [1 mark]
2. Use two uniform wires of the same material and cross-sectional area but different measured lengths. Keep their temperature the same, for example by taking brief readings and disconnecting between trials. Use the same test voltage. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Length, cross-sectional area and material all differ. A current/resistance difference could be due to any of them, so length has not been isolated.

Use two uniform wires of the same material and cross-sectional area but different measured lengths. Keep their temperature the same, for example by taking brief readings and disconnecting between trials. Use the same test voltage.

questions.competency_rationale: Identify confounding variables and redesign a causal comparison.

questions.text: A uniform wire is 1.5 m long, has cross-sectional area 0.30 mm² and resistance 2.0 Ω. (i) Express its area in m². (1 mark) (ii) Calculate the resistivity of its material at the test temperature. (1 mark)
questions.competency_rationale: Routine unit conversion and substitution; classified foundational.

questions.text: Two ammeters in a single steady series loop read the same current, one just before and one just after a heater. The heater nevertheless transfers electrical energy to its surroundings. (i) Use the readings to assess the claim “the heater uses up electric charge”. (1 mark) (ii) Explain what the source supplies and what changes as charge passes through the heater. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. Equal currents mean equal charge per second enters and leaves. Charge is not being used up or accumulating in the heater. [1 mark]
2. The source supplies electrical energy, not a continuing consumption of charge. Across the heater energy is transferred as heat; a charge Q transfers VQ while the charge itself is conserved. [1 mark]

questions.text: Drawings I and II in the figure use the same three resistor values and are each connected across a separate ideal 8 V source at terminals A and B. Dots denote joins. A student treats drawing II as three resistors in series because its components are spread around the page. (i) Identify the two endpoints of each resistor in each drawing, using node N where shown. (1 mark) (ii) Find the equivalent resistance in each drawing. (1 mark) (iii) Decide whether the sources deliver the same current and justify your answer numerically. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. In both drawings the 2 Ω resistor joins A to N, while both 6 Ω and 3 Ω join N to B. There is a junction at N, so the three resistors are not all in series. [1 mark]
2. In each drawing 6 Ω and 3 Ω are parallel: Rp = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2 Ω. The 2 Ω resistor is in series with this pair, so Req = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω in each. [1 mark]
3. Yes. Each source current is I = 8/4 = 2 A. The two drawings have the same connections and terminal resistance despite their different shapes. [1 mark]

questions.text: Use the switch positions and resistor values in the supplied figure. The ideal source is 6 V. (i) With both K₀ and K₁ closed, determine the source current. (1 mark) (ii) Keep K₀ closed but open K₁: determine the source current and state what happens to the current in resistor X, explaining why. (1 mark) (iii) Close K₁ and open K₀: determine the source current and explain why the effect differs from opening K₁ alone. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. Each 12 Ω branch carries 6/12 = 0.50 A; source current is 0.50 + 0.50 = 1.0 A. [1 mark]
2. Opening K₁ breaks only the Y branch. Source current becomes 0.50 A. X still spans the full 6 V and its current stays 0.50 A. [1 mark]
3. Opening K₀ gives source current 0 A because K₀ is in the common series lead and breaks the supply path for both branches. K₁ controls only Y, whereas K₀ controls both. [1 mark]

questions.text: The figure shows three uniform cylindrical wires of the same material at the same temperature. Their marked dimensions, not the apparent drawing sizes, are authoritative. (i) Find RX : RY : RZ. (1 mark) (ii) Select the two wires which give equal current when separately connected to the same ideal voltage source, with a reason. (1 mark) (iii) Can all three have the same resistivity despite the result in (i)? Explain. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. Since area is proportional to diameter squared, RX : RY : RZ = L/d² : 2L/(2d)² : 4L/(2d)² = 1 : 1/2 : 1, or 2 : 1 : 2. [1 mark]
2. X and Z have equal resistance and therefore equal current I = V/R at the same voltage. Y carries twice either current. [1 mark]
3. Yes. All have the same material and temperature, so their resistivity is the same. Different L/A changes resistance, not resistivity. [1 mark]

questions.text: The figure is an attempted resistance-measurement circuit. Its ideal voltmeter reads 6.0 V and its ideal ammeter reads 1.5 A with the switch closed. A report claims that the resistor labelled R is therefore 4 Ω. (i) Explain the connection error that invalidates the claim. (1 mark) (ii) Use the readings to determine R correctly. (1 mark) (iii) State how to reconnect the ammeter to measure only the current through R while retaining the voltmeter position. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. The ammeter is in the common lead before the junction, so it measures current through both R and the 6 Ω branch. 6.0/1.5 = 4 Ω is the parallel equivalent, not R. [1 mark]
2. The 6 Ω branch carries 6/6 = 1 A. R carries 1.5 − 1.0 = 0.50 A. Thus R = 6/0.50 = 12 Ω. [1 mark]
3. Move the ammeter into the R branch, in series with R, not into the other branch or across R. Replace its old common-lead position with an ideal wire. Leave the voltmeter across the two common nodes. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: The ammeter is in the common lead before the junction, so it measures current through both R and the 6 Ω branch. 6.0/1.5 = 4 Ω is the parallel equivalent, not R.

questions.text: Two resistors of 3 Ω and 6 Ω are tested for 60 s. (i) When connected in series, find the ratio H3Ω : H6Ω of heat produced, explaining the controlled quantity. (1 mark) (ii) When connected in parallel across the same ideal source, find that ratio and explain why it reverses. (1 mark) (iii) State Joule’s heating formula in terms of current, resistance and time. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. In series the current and time are equal. H = I²Rt therefore gives H3Ω : H6Ω = 3 : 6 = 1 : 2. [1 mark]
2. In parallel the voltage and time are equal, while currents differ. H = V²t/R gives H3Ω : H6Ω = (1/3) : (1/6) = 2 : 1. [1 mark]
3. Joule’s law: H = I²Rt, with H in joules when I is in amperes, R in ohms and t in seconds. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: In series the current and time are equal. H = I²Rt therefore gives H3Ω : H6Ω = 3 : 6 = 1 : 2.
In parallel the voltage and time are equal, while currents differ. H = V²t/R gives H3Ω : H6Ω = (1/3) : (1/6) = 2 : 1.
Joule’s law: H = I²Rt, with H in joules when I is in amperes, R in ohms and t in seconds.

questions.competency_rationale: Only (i) and (ii) count: controlled-current versus controlled-voltage comparison. Formula recall in (iii) is foundational.

questions.text: A display must remain on continuously for 4 h. Plan A uses a 30 W lamp for all 4 h. Plan B uses an 18 W lamp for the first 3 h and a 42 W lamp for the final 1 h. All operate at their stated powers; both plans meet the lighting requirement. (i) Calculate the energy for each plan in kWh. (1 mark) (ii) A budget allows at most 0.10 kWh. Select the feasible plan and state its energy margin below the budget. (1 mark) (iii) At ₹8 per kWh, find the cost saving of that plan relative to the other. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. EA = 0.030 × 4 = 0.120 kWh. EB = (0.018 × 3) + (0.042 × 1) = 0.096 kWh. [1 mark]
2. Only B meets the 0.10 kWh cap, with a margin of 0.100 − 0.096 = 0.004 kWh. A exceeds it by 0.020 kWh. [1 mark]
3. The saving is (0.120 − 0.096) × ₹8 = ₹0.192 (19.2 paise). Equivalently the costs are ₹0.960 and ₹0.768. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Only B meets the 0.10 kWh cap, with a margin of 0.100 − 0.096 = 0.004 kWh. A exceeds it by 0.020 kWh.
The saving is (0.120 − 0.096) × ₹8 = ₹0.192 (19.2 paise). Equivalently the costs are ₹0.960 and ₹0.768.

questions.competency_rationale: Only part (ii) receives 1 mark for the feasibility and margin decision. Energy calculations and multiplying the energy saving by the tariff are foundational arithmetic.

questions.text: An ideal 12 V supply feeds three parallel branches of 6 Ω, 12 Ω and 24 Ω. A fault makes exactly one entire branch open; all other components stay unchanged. The total current falls from 3.5 A to 2.5 A. (i) Identify the open branch using the size of the change. (1 mark) (ii) Predict the currents in the two intact branches. (1 mark) (iii) An ideal voltmeter is placed across the terminals of the broken branch. Predict its reading and explain why zero current does not imply zero voltage here. (1 mark)
questions.answer:
1. The missing current is 3.5 − 2.5 = 1.0 A. The intact branch currents would be 12/6 = 2 A, 12/12 = 1 A and 12/24 = 0.5 A; therefore the 12 Ω branch is open. [1 mark]
2. The 6 Ω branch still carries 2.0 A and the 24 Ω branch 0.50 A. Their sum is 2.50 A because they retain 12 V across them. [1 mark]
3. The voltmeter reads 12 V: the broken branch’s terminals are still connected to opposite source terminals. An open path prevents current but does not require its terminal potential difference to be zero. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: The missing current is 3.5 − 2.5 = 1.0 A. The intact branch currents would be 12/6 = 2 A, 12/12 = 1 A and 12/24 = 0.5 A; therefore the 12 Ω branch is open.
The 6 Ω branch still carries 2.0 A and the 24 Ω branch 0.50 A. Their sum is 2.50 A because they retain 12 V across them.

The voltmeter reads 12 V: the broken branch’s terminals are still connected to opposite source terminals. An open path prevents current but does not require its terminal potential difference to be zero.

questions.competency_rationale: Parts (i) and (iii) receive 2 marks for fault identification and interpreting nonzero voltage across an open path. Part (ii) is routine intact-branch current calculation.

questions.text: A test load must draw exactly 1.0 A from an ideal 12 V source. You must use all four available identical 12 Ω resistors, each rated for a maximum continuous power of 4.0 W. Only series and parallel connections are allowed; do not bypass a resistor. (i) Determine the required equivalent resistance. (1 mark) (ii) Design a suitable network: describe every branch connection clearly or draw a labelled circuit, and verify its equivalent resistance. (2 marks) (iii) Verify the power dissipated by each resistor and decide whether the design is acceptable. (1 mark) (iv) For your unchanged design, find the largest supply voltage permitted by the individual 4.0 W ratings. Give an exact or suitably rounded value. (1 mark)
questions.topic: Network design with individual power limit
questions.answer:
1. Required Req = V/I = 12/1.0 = 12 Ω. [1 mark]
2. One design: connect two 12 Ω resistors in series in branch 1 and the other two in series in branch 2; connect these 24 Ω branches in parallel across the source. Each resistor is used without a bypass. Equivalently, connect two parallel pairs in series. Award 1 mark for a complete valid connection description or diagram. [1 mark]
3. For the first design Req = (24 × 24)/(24 + 24) = 12 Ω, giving exactly 1.0 A. For the equivalent alternative, each parallel pair is 6 Ω and 6 + 6 = 12 Ω. Award 1 mark for verification. [1 mark]
4. The current divides equally: each resistor carries 0.50 A and has 6 V across it. Its power is (0.50)² × 12 = 3.0 W, below 4.0 W. All four therefore comply; total power is 12 W, matching VI. [1 mark]
5. In either valid design each resistor receives half the source voltage. Set (Vmax/2)²/12 = 4, giving Vmax² = 192 and Vmax = 8√3 V ≈ 13.86 V. At this limit each resistor dissipates 4 W. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Required Req = V/I = 12/1.0 = 12 Ω.

Each resistor is used without a bypass. Equivalently, connect two parallel pairs in series. Award 1 mark for a complete valid connection description or diagram.

In either valid design each resistor receives half the source voltage. Set (Vmax/2)²/12 = 4, giving Vmax² = 192 and Vmax = 8√3 V ≈ 13.86 V. At this limit each resistor dissipates 4 W.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is foundational. Parts (ii)–(iv) synthesize a topology, check actual power distribution and infer the limiting voltage; only these four marks count.

questions.text: The figure shows a series test chain connected across an ideal 12 V source. Only the three labelled resistors can be faulty; wires, source and ideal meters are sound. Test 1: the source current is zero. Voltage measurements are VPQ = 0 V, VQR = 12 V and VRS = 0 V (magnitudes). Exactly one resistor has become a complete open circuit. (i) Identify it and explain all three readings. (2 marks) (ii) After replacing it with an intact resistor of its labelled value, calculate the source current and the voltage across the 8 Ω resistor. (1 mark) Test 2 is a separate fault after full repair: an accidental ideal wire bypasses exactly one resistor and source current becomes 1.0 A. (iii) Identify the bypassed resistor using equivalent resistance, and predict its voltage. (2 marks)
questions.topic: Series open fault versus bypass fault
questions.answer:
1. The 8 Ω resistor between Q and R is open. With zero current, each intact finite resistor has voltage IR = 0, explaining VPQ = VRS = 0. Thus P and Q are at the positive-terminal potential, while R and S are at the negative-terminal potential; the entire 12 V appears across the break. Award 1 for identification and 1 for this consistent explanation. [2 marks]
2. After repair Req = 4 + 8 + 12 = 24 Ω; source current is 12/24 = 0.50 A. The voltage across 8 Ω is 0.50 × 8 = 4.0 V. [1 mark]
3. Test 2 gives Req = 12/1.0 = 12 Ω. Compared with the intact 24 Ω chain, 12 Ω has been removed electrically; therefore the 12 Ω resistor is bypassed. The ideal wire joins its terminals, so its voltage is 0 V and no current flows through that resistor itself. Award 1 for the equivalent-resistance deduction and 1 for the identified bypass with zero-voltage explanation. [2 marks]

marking_scheme.step: The 8 Ω resistor between Q and R is open. With zero current, each intact finite resistor has voltage IR = 0, explaining VPQ = VRS = 0. Thus P and Q are at the positive-terminal potential, while R and S are at the negative-terminal potential; the entire 12 V appears across the break. Award 1 for identification and 1 for this consistent explanation.
After repair Req = 4 + 8 + 12 = 24 Ω; source current is 12/24 = 0.50 A. The voltage across 8 Ω is 0.50 × 8 = 4.0 V.

Test 2 gives Req = 12/1.0 = 12 Ω. Compared with the intact 24 Ω chain, 12 Ω has been removed electrically; therefore the 12 Ω resistor is bypassed. The ideal wire joins its terminals, so its voltage is 0 V and no current flows through that resistor itself. Award 1 for the equivalent-resistance deduction and 1 for the identified bypass with zero-voltage explanation.

questions.competency_rationale: Parts (i) and (iii) receive 4 marks for open-versus-bypass diagnosis from evidence. Part (ii), the repaired series calculation, is foundational.

questions.text: A small resistive warming plate can use either mode F, one 12 Ω element across 12 V, or mode S, two identical 12 Ω elements in series across 12 V. The element resistances remain constant. All electrical energy generated in the active elements reaches the plate; ignore other losses. The plate needs 720 J within 90 s. (i) Calculate the total power in each mode. (2 marks) (ii) Determine which mode can meet the deadline, using its heating time. (1 mark) (iii) A student claims the lower-power mode necessarily uses less electrical energy to deliver the same 720 J. Evaluate the claim and find the charge delivered by the source for a complete delivery of 720 J in each mode, allowing mode S to run beyond the deadline. (2 marks)
questions.topic: Heating time, energy and charge trade-off
questions.answer:
1. Mode F has R = 12 Ω, so PF = V²/R = 144/12 = 12 W. [1 mark]
2. Mode S has R = 24 Ω, so PS = 144/24 = 6 W. [1 mark]
3. tF = 720/12 = 60 s, while tS = 720/6 = 120 s. Only F meets the 90 s deadline. [1 mark]
4. The claim is false under the stated loss-free transfer assumption: both require 720 J for a complete delivery. Lower power means a longer time, not less required energy. [1 mark]
5. Q = W/V = 720/12 = 60 C for either complete delivery, although F delivers this in 60 s and S in 120 s. This also follows from It: 1 A × 60 s or 0.5 A × 120 s. [1 mark]

Mode S has R = 24 Ω, so PS = 144/24 = 6 W.
tF = 720/12 = 60 s, while tS = 720/6 = 120 s. Only F meets the 90 s deadline.
The claim is false under the stated loss-free transfer assumption: both require 720 J for a complete delivery. Lower power means a longer time, not less required energy.

questions.competency_rationale: Only the deadline comparison and rejection of the lower-power/less-energy claim receive 2 marks. The two power calculations and Q=W/V substitution are foundational.

questions.text: A technician receives a sealed two-terminal box containing exactly two intact 18 Ω resistors, connected either in series or in parallel. An ideal source and ideal ammeter give these steady test records at constant temperature: 3.0 V → 0.333… A; 6.0 V → 0.666… A. Later, at the same 6.0 V, the current becomes 0.333… A. Exactly one internal resistor has become a complete open circuit; no other connection has changed. (i) Infer the original arrangement from both initial readings. (1 mark) (ii) Explain the later reading by calculating the new resistance and relating it to the stated failure. (1 mark) (iii) After the fault, the technician proposes doubling the voltage to restore the former total current. If each resistor has a 5 W maximum power rating, assess this proposal quantitatively. (2 marks)
questions.topic: Case study: sealed-box connectivity and repair risk
questions.answer:
1. Both readings give V/I = 9 Ω. Two 18 Ω resistors produce 9 Ω in parallel, whereas series would give 36 Ω. They were therefore parallel. [1 mark]
2. The later equivalent resistance is 6/(1/3) = 18 Ω. One parallel branch has opened, leaving the single intact 18 Ω branch carrying 1/3 A. [1 mark]
3. Doubling the voltage to 12 V would indeed give 12/18 = 2/3 A, equal to the former total current, but this current now all passes through one resistor. [1 mark]
4. Its power would be 12²/18 = 8 W, exceeding its 5 W rating. Reject the proposal even though it restores source current; replace the failed resistor or use a lower safe voltage instead. [1 mark]

The later equivalent resistance is 6/(1/3) = 18 Ω. One parallel branch has opened, leaving the single intact 18 Ω branch carrying 1/3 A.
