questions.competency_rationale: The initial table identifies hidden topology, the changed reading identifies its surviving path, and the proposed workaround must be tested against a component rating.

questions.text: A club builds a low-voltage sign from two resistive strips connected as parallel branches across an ideal 10 V source. Strip A has resistance 20 Ω and strip B 50 Ω. Each branch has its own ideal series switch, and there is a master switch in the common supply lead. In a trial, both strips operate for the first 4 min; only A operates for the next 2 min; then the master switch is opened. All resistances remain constant. A log states that opening B’s switch should reduce A’s current, and also claims that total source energy for the 6 min was 1800 J. (i) Assess the current claim with a value and reason. (1 mark) (ii) Calculate total source energy and decide whether the energy log is correct. (2 marks) (iii) Explain why opening the master switch, unlike opening B’s branch switch, turns both strips off. (1 mark)
questions.topic: Case study: independent control and energy logging
questions.answer:
1. The current claim is false. A remains directly across 10 V, so its current stays 10/20 = 0.50 A when B is switched off; source current falls, not A’s current. [1 mark]
2. PA = 10²/20 = 5 W and PB = 10²/50 = 2 W. During 4 min with both on, E1 = (5 + 2) × 240 = 1680 J. [1 mark]
3. During 2 min with only A, E2 = 5 × 120 = 600 J. Total E = 2280 J, so the 1800 J log is incorrect by 480 J. [1 mark]
4. The master switch is in the common lead needed by both complete paths. Opening it disconnects the source from both branches. B’s switch breaks only the B path. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: The current claim is false. A remains directly across 10 V, so its current stays 10/20 = 0.50 A when B is switched off; source current falls, not A’s current.
PA = 10²/20 = 5 W and PB = 10²/50 = 2 W. During 4 min with both on, E1 = (5 + 2) × 240 = 1680 J.
During 2 min with only A, E2 = 5 × 120 = 600 J. Total E = 2280 J, so the 1800 J log is incorrect by 480 J.
The master switch is in the common lead needed by both complete paths. Opening it disconnects the source from both branches. B’s switch breaks only the B path.

questions.competency_rationale: Parts (i), the second mark of (ii), and (iii) receive 3 marks for branch independence, reconciling the interval log and master-switch reasoning. The first energy-calculation mark is foundational.

questions.text: A student claims that a wire whose resistance changes must have changed its material. An intact uniform wire initially has length L, cross-sectional area A and resistance 10 Ω. It is stretched uniformly to length 2L without loss of material, so its volume LA stays constant. At the original temperature the stretched wire draws 0.10 A from an ideal 4.0 V source. It is then cut into two equal pieces, and those pieces are connected in parallel across the same source. Ignore contact resistance. (i) Use volume conservation to find the stretched area and, under the hypothesis that resistivity is unchanged, predict its resistance. (1 mark) (ii) Use the measured current to assess whether a material change is needed to explain the observation. (1 mark) (iii) Find the equivalent resistance after cutting and reconnecting, and compare the new source current with that of the original unstretched wire at 4.0 V. (2 marks)
questions.topic: Case study: material inference and reconnection
questions.answer:
1. Constant volume gives L A = (2L) Anew, so Anew = A/2. At unchanged resistivity Rnew/Rold = (2L/L)/(Anew/A) = 2/(1/2) = 4, hence Rnew = 40 Ω. [1 mark]
2. The measured resistance is 4.0/0.10 = 40 Ω, agreeing with the unchanged-resistivity prediction. The geometry change is sufficient; the reading does not require or establish a material change. [1 mark]
3. Each half of the stretched wire has length L and area A/2, so each has resistance 20 Ω. In parallel their equivalent resistance is 20/2 = 10 Ω. [1 mark]
4. New source current is 4.0/10 = 0.40 A. The original unstretched wire also drew 4.0/10 = 0.40 A, so the total source current is restored, although each new branch carries 0.20 A. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Constant volume gives L A = (2L) Anew, so Anew = A/2. At unchanged resistivity Rnew/Rold = (2L/L)/(Anew/A) = 2/(1/2) = 4, hence Rnew = 40 Ω.
The measured resistance is 4.0/0.10 = 40 Ω, agreeing with the unchanged-resistivity prediction. The geometry change is sufficient; the reading does not require or establish a material change.
Each half of the stretched wire has length L and area A/2, so each has resistance 20 Ω. In parallel their equivalent resistance is 20/2 = 10 Ω.
New source current is 4.0/10 = 0.40 A. The original unstretched wire also drew 4.0/10 = 0.40 A, so the total source current is restored, although each new branch carries 0.20 A.

questions.competency_rationale: Parts (i), (ii), and the reconnection-resistance mark in (iii) receive 3 marks for conserved-volume geometry, hypothesis/evidence comparison and topology change. The final current substitution/comparison is conservatively foundational.

questions.text: A net 5.0 × 10¹⁸ electrons pass a cross-section of a wire in one direction during 4.0 s. The magnitude of the charge on each electron is e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. What is the magnitude of the average current? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: B. The magnitude of net charge is Q = Ne = (5.0 × 10¹⁸)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 0.80 C. Hence I = Q/t = 0.80/4.0 = 0.20 A. The electron’s negative sign concerns direction, not the requested magnitude. The 0.80 value is charge, 3.2 multiplies rather than divides by time, and 1.25 is not Q/t. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: The magnitude of net charge is Q = Ne = (5.0 × 10¹⁸)(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 0.80 C. Hence I = Q/t = 0.80/4.0 = 0.20 A. The electron’s negative sign concerns direction, not the requested magnitude. The 0.80 value is charge, 3.2 multiplies rather than divides by time, and 1.25 is not Q/t.

questions.competency_rationale: Foundational use of Q = Ne followed by I = Q/t; the supplied electron charge removes any need for recalled numerical constants.
ncert_refs: §11.1, printed p.172: charge of an electron and I = Q/t

questions.text: Which statement gives the SI definition of a potential difference of one volt between two points? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: D. One volt means one joule of work per coulomb transferred between the two points: 1 V = 1 J/C. Option A defines an ampere; B defines a watt; C divides work by current rather than by charge and does not define a volt. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: One volt means one joule of work per coulomb transferred between the two points: 1 V = 1 J/C. Option A defines an ampere; B defines a watt; C divides work by current rather than by charge and does not define a volt.

questions.competency_rationale: Foundational recognition of the SI volt definition; no numerical W/Q substitution or competency credit.
ncert_refs: §11.2, printed p.173: definition of one volt, 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹
options: One coulomb of charge passes a cross-section each second.
One joule of energy is transferred each second.
One joule of work is done for each ampere of current.
One joule of work is done in moving one coulomb of charge between the points.

questions.text: During stage X, 90 C passes in 30 s; during stage Y, 120 C passes in 60 s. The current is steady within each stage. Which statement is correct? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: A. IX = 90/30 = 3 A and IY = 120/60 = 2 A. Hence X has 1.5 times the current of Y despite transferring less total charge. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: IX = 90/30 = 3 A and IY = 120/60 = 2 A. Hence X has 1.5 times the current of Y despite transferring less total charge.

questions.competency_rationale: Although presented as a comparison, this is only two direct I = Q/t substitutions; no competency credit claimed.
options: X has 1.5 times the current of Y
Y has twice the current of X
Y has 4/3 times the current of X

questions.text: The figure gives I against V for resistive devices X and Y. Each must operate continuously at 6 V for 10 min. A source can supply at most 1500 J for that interval. Which choice is possible? Read the graph; do not assume that the steeper line means greater resistance. [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: C. At 6 V the graph gives IX = 0.60 A and IY = 0.30 A. EX = 6 × 0.60 × 600 = 2160 J; EY = 6 × 0.30 × 600 = 1080 J. Only Y stays within 1500 J. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: At 6 V the graph gives IX = 0.60 A and IY = 0.30 A. EX = 6 × 0.60 × 600 = 2160 J; EY = 6 × 0.30 × 600 = 1080 J. Only Y stays within 1500 J.

questions.competency_rationale: Student must read the I-vertical graph, connect the current to energy, and test two alternatives against a cap.

diagram_image.alt: Current-versus-voltage plots for devices X and Y, with labelled axes and scales.

questions.text: The figure shows two uniform wires of the same material and temperature; dimensions, not drawing scale, are authoritative. They carry the same steady current for the same time in separate tests. Which prediction is correct? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: B. Y has twice the length but four times the area, so RY/RX = 2/4 = 1/2. At equal I and t, H = I²Rt gives HY/HX = 1/2. The material and temperature are unchanged, so resistivity is unchanged. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Y has twice the length but four times the area, so RY/RX = 2/4 = 1/2. At equal I and t, H = I²Rt gives HY/HX = 1/2. The material and temperature are unchanged, so resistivity is unchanged.

questions.competency_rationale: Requires using diameter squared in area, then choosing the fixed-current heat relationship rather than the fixed-voltage one.
options: Y produces twice the heat of X
Y produces half the heat of X
Y produces the same heat as X
Y produces one-quarter the heat and has lower resistivity

diagram_image.alt: Dimensioned cylindrical wires X and Y made from the same material.

questions.text: Two controlled drying trials produce the same accepted result. Trial A draws 800 W for 9 min. Trial B draws 500 W for 12 min, followed by 20 W for 15 min. All stated powers are actual constant input powers during their intervals. Which trial uses less electrical energy? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: D. EA = 800 × 9/60 = 120 Wh. EB = 500 × 12/60 + 20 × 15/60 = 105 Wh. Trial B uses 15 Wh less; the same accepted outcome permits a meaningful energy comparison. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: EA = 800 × 9/60 = 120 Wh. EB = 500 × 12/60 + 20 × 15/60 = 105 Wh. Trial B uses 15 Wh less; the same accepted outcome permits a meaningful energy comparison.

questions.competency_rationale: Must include a low-power after-run and compare complete schedules, not just nameplate power.

questions.text: A fixed-resistance warming tile is rated 60 W at 12 V. At 6 V it must supply 900 J of heat, all of which is useful. Which time is required? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: A. R = 12²/60 = 2.4 Ω. At 6 V, P = 6²/2.4 = 15 W. The time is 900/15 = 60 s, not 15 s from the rated power. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: R = 12²/60 = 2.4 Ω. At 6 V, P = 6²/2.4 = 15 W. The time is 900/15 = 60 s, not 15 s from the rated power.

questions.competency_rationale: Transfers a rating to a new voltage and then uses the heat target; power is not held at its rating.

questions.text: A constant-temperature resistor gives the following readings: (V in volts, I in amperes) = (1.5, 0.15), (3.0, 0.30), (4.5, 0.90), (6.0, 0.60). Exactly one current was copied incorrectly. Which corrected entry restores consistency with the other three pairs? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: C. The first, second and fourth pairs all give V/I = 10 Ω. At 4.5 V the consistent current is 4.5/10 = 0.45 A. Replacing 0.90 A by 0.45 A restores the constant ratio. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: The first, second and fourth pairs all give V/I = 10 Ω. At 4.5 V the consistent current is 4.5/10 = 0.45 A. Replacing 0.90 A by 0.45 A restores the constant ratio.

questions.competency_rationale: Identifies the common resistance from several measurements and diagnoses a transcription error.
options: At 1.5 V, change 0.15 A to 0.30 A
At 3.0 V, change 0.30 A to 0.60 A
At 4.5 V, change 0.90 A to 0.45 A
At 6.0 V, change 0.60 A to 1.20 A

questions.text: A supplier lists the electrical resistivity of a wire material at 20 °C. An engineer wants to use that value for a heating element operating at a much higher temperature. Which statement is correct? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: B. B is correct. Resistivity is a property of a material at a specified temperature, and can change when that temperature changes. The room-temperature value is not guaranteed to describe the hot element. No universal zero value follows from heating, and dividing by length does not supply temperature dependence. The question supplies no law for calculating the hot value or its direction of change. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: B is correct. Resistivity is a property of a material at a specified temperature, and can change when that temperature changes. The room-temperature value is not guaranteed to describe the hot element. No universal zero value follows from heating, and dividing by length does not supply temperature dependence. The question supplies no law for calculating the hot value or its direction of change.

questions.competency_rationale: Foundational practical recognition that a tabulated resistivity is temperature-specific; no numerical trend, material classification or experimental diagnosis is required.
ncert_refs: §11.5, printed p.179: resistance and resistivity vary with temperature; Table 11.2 values at 20 °C
options: The listed value must apply at every temperature because the material name is unchanged.
The operating-temperature resistivity is needed; resistivity can vary with temperature.
The resistivity must become zero whenever the element is hot.
The hotter resistivity can be found by dividing the listed value by the wire length.

questions.text: In the supplied circuit, switch S is initially open. It is then closed while the ideal source stays at 12 V. Which change occurs? All resistances stay constant. [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: D. With S open only the 12 Ω branch conducts, drawing 12/12 = 1 A. Closing S adds a 6 Ω branch drawing 2 A; total current becomes 3 A, but the 12 Ω branch remains across 12 V and stays at 1 A. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: With S open only the 12 Ω branch conducts, drawing 12/12 = 1 A. Closing S adds a 6 Ω branch drawing 2 A; total current becomes 3 A, but the 12 Ω branch remains across 12 V and stays at 1 A.

questions.competency_rationale: Must trace a branch switch and distinguish branch current from total source current.
options: The current in the 12 Ω resistor becomes 3 A
The source current stays at 1 A
The source current becomes 3 A; the 12 Ω current stays 1 A

diagram_image.alt: A 12 V source connected to two resistor branches, one containing switch S.

questions.text: For a fixed resistor, a second trial uses half the first trial’s current but lasts twice as long. What is the ratio Hsecond/Hfirst of heat generated? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: A. Hsecond/Hfirst = (1/2)² × 2 = 1/2. Doubling the duration does not compensate for reducing current by a factor of two. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Hsecond/Hfirst = (1/2)² × 2 = 1/2. Doubling the duration does not compensate for reducing current by a factor of two.

questions.competency_rationale: This is a routine proportional substitution in H = I²Rt; conservatively classified foundational.

questions.text: Two identical fixed resistors are connected in series across an ideal voltage source for time t. They are then connected in parallel across the same source. For how long must the parallel arrangement run to use the same total electrical energy? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: C. For individual resistance R, Rs = 2R and Rp = R/2. At the same voltage Pparallel/Pseries = Rs/Rp = 4. Equal energies require tparallel = t/4. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: For individual resistance R, Rs = 2R and Rp = R/2. At the same voltage Pparallel/Pseries = Rs/Rp = 4. Equal energies require tparallel = t/4.

questions.competency_rationale: Combines equivalent-resistance comparison with equal-energy duration, rather than merely calculating resistance.

questions.text: A steady 2 A is measured immediately before and immediately after a resistor. The resistor transfers 10 J of electrical energy each second as heat. Which interpretation is consistent with both observations? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: B. In steady operation 2 C enters and 2 C leaves each second, so charge is not consumed. The transferred energy per coulomb is 10/2 = 5 J/C, consistent with a 5 V drop across the resistor. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: In steady operation 2 C enters and 2 C leaves each second, so charge is not consumed. The transferred energy per coulomb is 10/2 = 5 J/C, consistent with a 5 V drop across the resistor.

questions.competency_rationale: Reconciles equal charge-flow rates with a nonzero energy transfer; rejects charge-consumption reasoning.
options: The resistor consumes 10 C each second
Charge flow is unchanged; 5 J is transferred per coulomb
The exiting current must actually be zero
Equal currents imply zero potential difference

questions.text: A voltmeter displays +0.4 V when its two leads touch. Across a resistor it displays 2.4 V while an accurate ammeter reads 0.50 A. Assuming this is a constant additive zero error, what should a student do? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: D. The meter overreads by 0.4 V. True voltage = 2.4 − 0.4 = 2.0 V and R = 2.0/0.50 = 4.0 Ω. Adding the offset or using the uncorrected reading would overestimate R. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: The meter overreads by 0.4 V. True voltage = 2.4 − 0.4 = 2.0 V and R = 2.0/0.50 = 4.0 Ω. Adding the offset or using the uncorrected reading would overestimate R.

questions.competency_rationale: Diagnoses the sign of an offset and corrects measured voltage before interpreting resistance.
options: Ignore the offset and report 4.8 Ω

questions.text: Which pair of properties explains why suitable alloys are commonly used for heating elements? [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: A. Suitable heating alloys generally have relatively high resistivity and do not oxidise readily at high temperatures. Low resistance alone or rapid oxidation would not justify their use. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Suitable heating alloys generally have relatively high resistivity and do not oxidise readily at high temperatures. Low resistance alone or rapid oxidation would not justify their use.

questions.competency_rationale: Recall of material properties from the textbook, not a data-based material selection task.
options: Relatively high resistivity and resistance to oxidation at high temperature
Very low melting point and rapid oxidation
Zero resistance and negligible heat production

questions.text: The graph gives the complete power schedule of a device over 8 min. An alternative draws a steady 300 W for all 8 min. Which comparison is correct? Use rectangular energy blocks, without calculus. [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: C. From the graph E = 600 × 2/60 + 200 × 4/60 + 0 × 2/60 = 33⅓ Wh. The alternative uses 300 × 8/60 = 40 Wh. The plotted schedule uses 6⅔ Wh less. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: From the graph E = 600 × 2/60 + 200 × 4/60 + 0 × 2/60 = 33⅓ Wh. The alternative uses 300 × 8/60 = 40 Wh. The plotted schedule uses 6⅔ Wh less.

questions.competency_rationale: Must read interval boundaries and compare areas as power × time, including the off interval.
options: The graph uses 6⅔ Wh less than the alternative
The graph uses 6⅔ Wh more than the alternative

diagram_image.alt: Power-versus-time schedule shown by horizontal segments over eight minutes.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): If the resistance of an element is doubled while its voltage and operating time are kept fixed, it produces twice as much heat.
Reason (R): At fixed voltage, the heat produced in time t is H = V²t/R.
Choose the appropriate shared assertion–reason option. [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: D. A is false: doubling R at fixed V and t halves heat. R is true, since H = VIt and I = V/R give H = V²t/R. Thus option D applies. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: A is false: doubling R at fixed V and t halves heat. R is true, since H = VIt and I = V/R give H = V²t/R. Thus option D applies.

questions.competency_rationale: The reason supplies H = V²t/R directly; testing a doubled denominator is foundational scaling.
options: both true and R correctly explains A
both true but R does not correctly explain A

questions.text:
Assertion (A): A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power.
Reason (R): An ideal ammeter is connected in series with the component whose current it measures.
Choose the appropriate shared assertion–reason option. [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: B. A is true because kWh is power multiplied by time. R is also true, but how an ammeter is connected does not explain the dimension of kWh. Hence B. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: A is true because kWh is power multiplied by time. R is also true, but how an ammeter is connected does not explain the dimension of kWh. Hence B.

questions.competency_rationale: Tests two foundational facts and their lack of explanatory relationship.
options: both true and R correctly explains A
both true but R does not correctly explain A

questions.text:
Assertion (A): In a steady series circuit, a heater does not make the current measured after it smaller than the current measured before it.
Reason (R): Charge does not accumulate in the heater during steady operation, so equal charge enters and leaves in each time interval.
Choose the appropriate shared assertion–reason option. [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: A. Both statements are true. No steady accumulation means equal entering and leaving charge per unit time; this directly explains the equal series currents. Energy is transferred but charge is conserved. Hence A. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: Both statements are true. No steady accumulation means equal entering and leaving charge per unit time; this directly explains the equal series currents. Energy is transferred but charge is conserved. Hence A.

questions.competency_rationale: Both the series-current fact and its conservation explanation are supplied; conservatively foundational.
options: both true and R correctly explains A
both true but R does not correctly explain A

questions.text:
Assertion (A): A fixed-resistance heater operated at half its rated voltage for twice a reference time transfers half the energy it would transfer at rated voltage for that reference time.
Reason (R): Halving the applied voltage halves the resistance of a fixed-resistance heater.
Choose the appropriate shared assertion–reason option. [1 mark]
questions.answer: Correct option: C. A is true: Enew/Ereference = (1/2)² × 2 = 1/2. R is false because the heater is explicitly fixed-resistance; lowering voltage lowers current, not its resistance. Hence C. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: A is true: Enew/Ereference = (1/2)² × 2 = 1/2. R is false because the heater is explicitly fixed-resistance; lowering voltage lowers current, not its resistance. Hence C.

questions.competency_rationale: Routine voltage/time scaling plus recognition of the explicitly fixed resistance; foundational.
options: both true and R correctly explains A
both true but R does not correctly explain A

questions.text: A controller supplies 0.40 A for 30 s and then 0.10 A for 90 s. (i) Find the total charge delivered. [1 mark] (ii) A student reports the average current as (0.40 + 0.10)/2 = 0.25 A. Test this report using the total charge and elapsed time. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) Q = 0.40 × 30 + 0.10 × 90 = 12 + 9 = 21 C. [1 mark]
(ii) Total time = 120 s. Average current = total charge/total time = 21/120 = 0.175 A. The proposed 0.25 A is wrong because the lower-current stage lasts three times as long. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Total time = 120 s. Average current = total charge/total time = 21/120 = 0.175 A. The proposed 0.25 A is wrong because the lower-current stage lasts three times as long.

questions.competency_rationale: The first mark is routine Q = It; the second tests an unweighted-average misconception using unequal durations.

questions.text: Device U transfers 240 J while 40 C passes through it; device V transfers 180 J while 20 C passes. (i) Calculate their potential differences. [1 mark] (ii) A student says U must have the higher voltage because it transfers more energy. Evaluate the claim. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) VU = 240/40 = 6 V; VV = 180/20 = 9 V. Award 0.5 mark for each. [1 mark]
(ii) The claim is false: V transfers 9 J/C, compared with U’s 6 J/C. More total energy does not imply a higher voltage when different amounts of charge pass. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) VU = 240/40 = 6 V; VV = 180/20 = 9 V. Award 0.5 mark for each.
(ii) The claim is false: V transfers 9 J/C, compared with U’s 6 J/C. More total energy does not imply a higher voltage when different amounts of charge pass.

questions.competency_rationale: Voltage calculations are foundational; the explanatory comparison distinguishes total energy from energy per coulomb.

questions.text: In the supplied experimental circuit, both meters are ideal and the 10 V source is ideal. (i) Predict the ammeter and voltmeter readings. [1 mark] (ii) A student divides the voltmeter reading by the ammeter reading and labels the result “the total resistance connected to the source”. Explain the error and give the resistance that this ratio actually measures. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) The resistors are in series: Rtotal = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω, so A reads 10/10 = 1 A. The voltmeter spans only the 6 Ω resistor and reads 1 × 6 = 6 V. Award 0.5 each. [1 mark]
(ii) The ratio is 6 V/1 A = 6 Ω, the resistance between the voltmeter’s connection nodes, not total resistance. Total resistance is 10 Ω; its calculation requires the source’s full 10 V. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) The resistors are in series: Rtotal = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω, so A reads 10/10 = 1 A. The voltmeter spans only the 6 Ω resistor and reads 1 × 6 = 6 V. Award 0.5 each.
(ii) The ratio is 6 V/1 A = 6 Ω, the resistance between the voltmeter’s connection nodes, not total resistance. Total resistance is 10 Ω; its calculation requires the source’s full 10 V.

questions.competency_rationale: Requires tracing the voltmeter nodes, calculating series current, and distinguishing component voltage from whole-circuit voltage.

diagram_image.alt: Series circuit with two resistors, an ammeter and a voltmeter attached to labelled nodes.

questions.text: For a resistor carrying a steady current I for time t at voltage V, (i) use W = VQ and Q = It to obtain the heat transferred, assuming all electrical energy becomes heat. [1 mark] (ii) Apply Ohm’s law to express this heat in terms of I, R and t, and state what must stay fixed when claiming that heat is proportional to resistance. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) H = W = VQ = V(It) = VIt, for the purely resistive device. [1 mark]
(ii) V = IR gives H = (IR)It = I²Rt. Heat is proportional to R only if current I and duration t are fixed. Award 0.5 for the expression and 0.5 for both conditions. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) H = W = VQ = V(It) = VIt, for the purely resistive device.
(ii) V = IR gives H = (IR)It = I²Rt. Heat is proportional to R only if current I and duration t are fixed. Award 0.5 for the expression and 0.5 for both conditions.

questions.competency_rationale: Standard derivation and the conditions of proportionality are foundational, not automatically competency.

questions.text: Two settings of a device both meet the same processing requirement: setting X draws 900 W for 8 min and setting Y draws 600 W for 13 min. The tariff is ₹8 per kWh with no other charges. (i) Which uses less energy, and by how much per run? [1 mark] (ii) Find the saving for 50 runs using the better setting. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) EX = 0.9 × 8/60 = 0.12 kWh; EY = 0.6 × 13/60 = 0.13 kWh. X uses 0.01 kWh less per run despite its higher power. [1 mark]
(ii) Energy saving over 50 runs = 50 × 0.01 = 0.50 kWh. Money saved = 0.50 × ₹8 = ₹4. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) EX = 0.9 × 8/60 = 0.12 kWh; EY = 0.6 × 13/60 = 0.13 kWh. X uses 0.01 kWh less per run despite its higher power.
(ii) Energy saving over 50 runs = 50 × 0.01 = 0.50 kWh. Money saved = 0.50 × ₹8 = ₹4.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) compares complete equal-outcome schedules. Part (ii) is a routine cost multiplication and receives no competency credit.

questions.text: A student compares two different wire materials at the same voltage. Wire A is twice as long as B and both have the same diameter. A carries less current, so the student concludes that A’s material has higher resistivity. (i) Is that conclusion guaranteed? Explain. [1 mark] (ii) Specify a controlled replacement comparison that would let current alone rank the two resistivities. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) No. Lower current implies higher resistance at the same voltage, but R = ρL/A. A’s greater length can itself cause its higher resistance, even for equal or somewhat lower resistivity. [1 mark]
(ii) Compare wires of the two materials with equal lengths and equal cross-sectional areas, at the same temperature and voltage. Then R is proportional to ρ, so the lower-current wire has higher resistivity. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) No. Lower current implies higher resistance at the same voltage, but R = ρL/A. A’s greater length can itself cause its higher resistance, even for equal or somewhat lower resistivity.

(ii) Compare wires of the two materials with equal lengths and equal cross-sectional areas, at the same temperature and voltage. Then R is proportional to ρ, so the lower-current wire has higher resistivity.

questions.competency_rationale: Detects length as a confounder and designs a comparison that isolates material.

questions.text: A uniform wire has resistivity 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m, length 0.80 m and area 0.20 mm². It forms a constant-resistance element. (i) Find its resistance. [1 mark] (ii) A replacement of the same material and length has twice the diameter. Decide whether it uses less energy during the same time at the same voltage, supporting your answer with resistance and energy ratios. [2 marks]
questions.answer:
(i) 0.20 mm² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ m². R = ρL/A = (1.2 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.80)/(2.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 4.8 Ω. [1 mark]
(ii) Doubling diameter multiplies area by four; replacement resistance is R/4 = 1.2 Ω. Award 1 mark for this chain. [1 mark]
At fixed V and t, E = V²t/R. The replacement uses four times the original energy, not less. Its lower resistance draws more current. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Doubling diameter multiplies area by four; replacement resistance is R/4 = 1.2 Ω. Award 1 mark for this chain.
At fixed V and t, E = V²t/R. The replacement uses four times the original energy, not less. Its lower resistance draws more current.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is routine; part (ii) transfers a diameter change through area and resistance into a voltage-controlled energy decision.

questions.text:
An ideal source maintains 12 V across a purely resistive element for 60 s. In a two-stage approximation to its measured behaviour, its resistance is 6 Ω for the first 30 s and 12 Ω for the next 30 s; treat each stage as constant and the transition as instantaneous. All electrical input energy becomes generated heat. This stated change overrides the paper’s usual fixed-resistance assumption.
(i) Calculate the heat generated in each stage and the total. [1 mark]
(ii) A student correctly finds the time-average current to be 1.5 A and the time-average resistance to be 9 Ω, then reports H = (1.5)² × 9 × 60 = 1215 J. Diagnose the error and quantify the discrepancy from the correct total. [1 mark]
(iii) Another student proposes H = 12 × 1.5 × 60 using the same average current. Is this method valid for this run? Explain using total charge or the two stage contributions, not calculus. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Piecewise heating and validity of average-value methods
questions.answer:
(i) First stage: I₁ = 12/6 = 2 A, H₁ = 12² × 30/6 = 720 J. Second stage: I₂ = 12/12 = 1 A, H₂ = 12² × 30/12 = 360 J. Total H = 720 + 360 = 1080 J. Award 0.5 for both stage heats and 0.5 for the total with working. [1 mark]
(ii) The actual pairs are (2 A, 6 Ω) and (1 A, 12 Ω). H = I²Rt must use the matching current and resistance for each constant stage; squaring the average current and multiplying by the separately averaged resistance does not preserve these stagewise products. The 1215 J report exceeds the correct total by 1215 − 1080 = 135 J. Award 0.5 for identifying this invalid replacement and 0.5 for the excess. [1 mark]
(iii) Yes, because the voltage remains 12 V throughout. Total charge Q = 2 × 30 + 1 × 30 = 90 C = Iaverage × 60. Thus H = VQ = 12 × 90 = 1080 J = 12 × 1.5 × 60. Award 0.5 for the fixed-voltage/total-charge justification and 0.5 for the matching total. An average current is not inherently invalid; its use depends on the energy expression and controlled quantities. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) First stage: I₁ = 12/6 = 2 A, H₁ = 12² × 30/6 = 720 J. Second stage: I₂ = 12/12 = 1 A, H₂ = 12² × 30/12 = 360 J. Total H = 720 + 360 = 1080 J. Award 0.5 for both stage heats and 0.5 for the total with working.

(ii) The actual pairs are (2 A, 6 Ω) and (1 A, 12 Ω). H = I²Rt must use the matching current and resistance for each constant stage; squaring the average current and multiplying by the separately averaged resistance does not preserve these stagewise products. The 1215 J report exceeds the correct total by 1215 − 1080 = 135 J. Award 0.5 for identifying this invalid replacement and 0.5 for the excess.

(iii) Yes, because the voltage remains 12 V throughout. Total charge Q = 2 × 30 + 1 × 30 = 90 C = Iaverage × 60. Thus H = VQ = 12 × 90 = 1080 J = 12 × 1.5 × 60. Award 0.5 for the fixed-voltage/total-charge justification and 0.5 for the matching total. An average current is not inherently invalid; its use depends on the energy expression and controlled quantities.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is routine stagewise substitution (0). Part (ii) diagnoses why multiplying separately averaged current and resistance misrepresents their paired stages (1). Part (iii) distinguishes a valid fixed-voltage average-current method using charge or additive energy, rather than rejecting all averages (1).
ncert_refs: §11.7, printed pp.188–189: H = VIt, H = I²Rt and current recalculation at known voltage
§11.5, printed p.179: resistance can vary with temperature

questions.text: A fixed-resistance mat is rated 90 W at 18 V. A technician wants it to generate 5400 J in no more than 90 s. Only ideal 12 V and 15 V sources are available, one used at a time. (i) Infer the mat resistance. [1 mark] (ii) Determine which source, if either, meets the target, calculating the required time for each. [2 marks]
questions.answer:
(i) R = 18²/90 = 3.6 Ω. [1 mark]
(ii) At 12 V, P = 12²/3.6 = 40 W and time = 5400/40 = 135 s, which misses the 90 s deadline. [1 mark]
At 15 V, P = 15²/3.6 = 62.5 W and time = 5400/62.5 = 86.4 s. Only the 15 V source meets the deadline. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) At 12 V, P = 12²/3.6 = 40 W and time = 5400/40 = 135 s, which misses the 90 s deadline.
At 15 V, P = 15²/3.6 = 62.5 W and time = 5400/62.5 = 86.4 s. Only the 15 V source meets the deadline.

questions.competency_rationale: The resistance-from-rating step is foundational; comparing both altered-voltage performances against a deadline earns two competency marks.

questions.text: The graph shows cumulative heat generated by resistors X and Y during a controlled test; the two straight lines have been measured independently. X is 6 Ω and Y is 12 Ω. One student says the graph proves equal currents; another says it is consistent with equal voltages. (i) Read the heat ratio HX:HY at 40 s. [1 mark] (ii) Use the heat and time to test both statements and identify the consistent condition, including its common electrical value. [2 marks]
questions.answer:
(i) At 40 s, HX = 240 J and HY = 120 J, so HX:HY = 2:1. [1 mark]
(ii) PX = 240/40 = 6 W and PY = 120/40 = 3 W. IX = √(6/6) = 1 A and IY = √(3/12) = 0.5 A; they are not equal. An equal-current test would instead make the 12 Ω resistor produce twice as much heat. [1 mark]
VX = IXRX = 1 × 6 = 6 V and VY = IYRY = 0.5 × 12 = 6 V. Thus the graph is consistent with equal 6 V supplies, not equal currents. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) At 40 s, HX = 240 J and HY = 120 J, so HX:HY = 2:1.
(ii) PX = 240/40 = 6 W and PY = 120/40 = 3 W. IX = √(6/6) = 1 A and IY = √(3/12) = 0.5 A; they are not equal. An equal-current test would instead make the 12 Ω resistor produce twice as much heat.
VX = IXRX = 1 × 6 = 6 V and VY = IYRY = 0.5 × 12 = 6 V. Thus the graph is consistent with equal 6 V supplies, not equal currents.

questions.competency_rationale: Reading the heat ratio in (i) is foundational. The two marks in (ii) interpret heating rates to reject equal current and identify the common voltage.

diagram_image.alt: Cumulative heat-versus-time graph for resistors X and Y.

questions.text: A 3 Ω resistor is in series with two 6 Ω resistors in parallel, across an ideal 12 V source. All resistances are fixed. One of the 6 Ω branches becomes open-circuit. (i) Find the current through the remaining 6 Ω resistor before and after this fault. [2 marks] (ii) Decide whether the heat it generates in a given time increases or decreases, and give the factor. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Fault consequences in a mixed circuit
questions.answer:
(i) Before the fault, parallel resistance is 3 Ω and total resistance 6 Ω. Source current is 12/6 = 2 A, shared equally: each 6 Ω resistor carries 1 A. [1 mark]
After the fault, the path is 3 Ω + 6 Ω = 9 Ω. The current in the remaining resistor is 12/9 = 4/3 A. [1 mark]
(ii) At the same R and t, Hafter/Hbefore = (4/3)²/1² = 16/9. Its heat increases by a factor of 16/9 even though total source current falls. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Before the fault, parallel resistance is 3 Ω and total resistance 6 Ω. Source current is 12/6 = 2 A, shared equally: each 6 Ω resistor carries 1 A.
After the fault, the path is 3 Ω + 6 Ω = 9 Ω. The current in the remaining resistor is 12/9 = 4/3 A.
(ii) At the same R and t, Hafter/Hbefore = (4/3)²/1² = 16/9. Its heat increases by a factor of 16/9 even though total source current falls.

questions.competency_rationale: The pre-fault baseline circuit calculation is foundational. Reconstructing the faulted circuit and explaining increased surviving-branch heat earn two competency marks.

questions.text: An ideal supply has two independent operating limits: instantaneous output power must not exceed 100 W, and total delivered energy during a session must not exceed 40 Wh. A 60 W task runs for 30 min and a 50 W task runs for 10 min; each draws its stated constant power while on. (i) Can they run simultaneously for the first 10 min? [1 mark] (ii) Can both be completed one after the other within the energy limit? [1 mark] (iii) Explain why satisfying one of these limits does not automatically satisfy the other. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) No. Their simultaneous power is 60 + 50 = 110 W, above 100 W. [1 mark]
(ii) Yes. Sequential power is at most 60 W and total energy is 60 × 30/60 + 50 × 10/60 = 30 + 8⅓ = 38⅓ Wh, below 40 Wh. [1 mark]
(iii) Power limits the rate of energy delivery; energy also depends on how long the tasks run. Short overlap can violate the power limit without exceeding the energy budget; a long low-power run can exceed an energy budget while staying below the power limit. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) No. Their simultaneous power is 60 + 50 = 110 W, above 100 W.
(ii) Yes. Sequential power is at most 60 W and total energy is 60 × 30/60 + 50 × 10/60 = 30 + 8⅓ = 38⅓ Wh, below 40 Wh.

(iii) Power limits the rate of energy delivery; energy also depends on how long the tasks run. Short overlap can violate the power limit without exceeding the energy budget; a long low-power run can exceed an energy budget while staying below the power limit.

questions.competency_rationale: Distinguishes a peak constraint from a time-accumulated constraint and selects a feasible schedule.

questions.text:
A resistor was previously measured as 20 Ω using trusted instruments. In a new test at the same temperature, an accurate voltmeter is connected directly across it. Suspect ammeter A displays 0.125 A at 2.0 V and 0.250 A at 4.0 V. Consider two explanations: the resistor has genuinely changed to a different fixed resistance and A is accurate; or the resistor is unchanged and A displays a constant multiple of the true current. Both meters have negligible loading, and readings are exact for this question.
(i) What resistance would be inferred if A’s readings were assumed accurate? [1 mark]
(ii) A is replaced, in the same series position, by independently calibrated ammeter B. With the resistor, temperature and measured voltages unchanged, B reads 0.100 A at 2.0 V and 0.200 A at 4.0 V. Which explanation does this evidence support? Determine the factor by which A multiplies the true current. [1 mark]
(iii) A student argues that A must be accurate because it reads zero when no current flows and its displayed-current-versus-voltage plot is a straight line through the origin. Explain why neither observation rules out the error identified in (ii). [1 mark]
questions.topic: Scale-factor meter error versus changed resistance
questions.answer:
(i) From A, R = 2.0/0.125 = 16 Ω; the second pair gives 4.0/0.250 = 16 Ω as well. The inferred value would therefore be 16 Ω, not the earlier 20 Ω. [1 mark]
(ii) Trusted B gives 2.0/0.100 = 20 Ω and 4.0/0.200 = 20 Ω, supporting unchanged resistance and an error in A. A/B = 0.125/0.100 = 0.250/0.200 = 1.25, so A displays 1.25 times the true current, an overreading of 25%. Award 0.5 for the diagnosis from B’s resistance and 0.5 for the consistent factor. [1 mark]
(iii) Multiplying a zero true current by 1.25 still gives zero, so a correct zero reading does not establish a correct scale. Also, for the 20 Ω resistor, Itrue = V/20 and IA = 1.25V/20 = V/16: multiplying every current by the same factor preserves a straight line through the origin but changes its slope. Award 0.5 for each explanation. The independently calibrated comparison, not either shape/zero test alone, exposes this error. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) From A, R = 2.0/0.125 = 16 Ω; the second pair gives 4.0/0.250 = 16 Ω as well. The inferred value would therefore be 16 Ω, not the earlier 20 Ω.

(ii) Trusted B gives 2.0/0.100 = 20 Ω and 4.0/0.200 = 20 Ω, supporting unchanged resistance and an error in A. A/B = 0.125/0.100 = 0.250/0.200 = 1.25, so A displays 1.25 times the true current, an overreading of 25%. Award 0.5 for the diagnosis from B’s resistance and 0.5 for the consistent factor.

(iii) Multiplying a zero true current by 1.25 still gives zero, so a correct zero reading does not establish a correct scale. Also, for the 20 Ω resistor, Itrue = V/20 and IA = 1.25V/20 = V/16: multiplying every current by the same factor preserves a straight line through the origin but changes its slope. Award 0.5 for each explanation. The independently calibrated comparison, not either shape/zero test alone, exposes this error.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is a routine V/I calculation (0). Part (ii) uses independent same-condition meter-swap evidence to discriminate a changed component from an instrument scale error (1). Part (iii) explains why a multiplicative error passes both zero and straight-line checks (1). No additive offset, contact resistance, heating anomaly or voltmeter-span error is involved.
ncert_refs: §11.1, printed p.172: ammeter measures current and is connected in series
§11.4 / Activity 11.1, printed pp.175–176: V/I measurements, resistance and straight-line relation at constant temperature

questions.text:
A workshop compares two complete programmes that tests have shown give the same accepted drying result. Programme A draws 1.2 kW for 6 min, then 80 W for 15 min. Programme B draws 750 W for 10 min, then 30 W for 20 min. Powers are actual constant input powers; all unlisted intervals draw zero power. There are 24 runs per day. The daily energy budget is 3.30 kWh and the tariff is ₹9 per kWh, with no other charges.
(i) Calculate the electrical energy of each complete programme per run. [2 marks]
(ii) Select the programme that fits the daily energy budget and show the daily margin or excess for each. [2 marks]
(iii) Find the daily cost saving from choosing the lower-energy programme, and explain why choosing solely by the largest stated power could mislead. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) A: 1.2 × 6/60 + 0.080 × 15/60 = 0.120 + 0.020 = 0.140 kWh per run. [1 mark]
B: 0.750 × 10/60 + 0.030 × 20/60 = 0.125 + 0.010 = 0.135 kWh per run. [1 mark]
(ii) A uses 24 × 0.140 = 3.36 kWh/day, exceeding the budget by 3.36 − 3.30 = 0.06 kWh. [1 mark]
B uses 24 × 0.135 = 3.24 kWh/day, leaving 3.30 − 3.24 = 0.06 kWh. Choose B, since only B fits the daily budget and both meet the process requirement. [1 mark]
(iii) Daily saving = (3.36 − 3.24) × ₹9 = ₹1.08. Award 0.5 for the cost and 0.5 for explaining that energy depends on each power AND its duration, including after-runs; the largest power by itself is insufficient. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) A uses 24 × 0.140 = 3.36 kWh/day, exceeding the budget by 3.36 − 3.30 = 0.06 kWh.
B uses 24 × 0.135 = 3.24 kWh/day, leaving 3.30 − 3.24 = 0.06 kWh. Choose B, since only B fits the daily budget and both meet the process requirement.

(iii) Daily saving = (3.36 − 3.24) × ₹9 = ₹1.08. Award 0.5 for the cost and 0.5 for explaining that energy depends on each power AND its duration, including after-runs; the largest power by itself is insufficient.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is routine accumulation of specified power-time blocks (0). Part (ii) tests both complete daily schedules against a cap (2). In part (iii), cost multiplication is foundational (0), but explaining why peak power alone is insufficient earns 0.5.

questions.text:
A purely resistive portable warmer is rated 48 W at 12 V. Its resistance is assumed unchanged at other voltages. A proposed source maintains 9 V at the warmer. For a particular task, exactly three-quarters of the electrical input energy reaches the useful load; the rest is lost to the surroundings. The load needs 4050 J of useful heat and the deadline is 4 min.
(i) Infer the warmer’s resistance and actual power at 9 V. [2 marks]
(ii) Calculate the electrical energy required and the time at 9 V. Does the proposal meet the deadline? [2 marks]
(iii) A student instead inserts 48 W into the time calculation because “the printed power cannot change”. Explain quantitatively why that prediction is wrong. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) R = 12²/48 = 3 Ω. [1 mark]
At 9 V, actual input power P = 9²/3 = 27 W (current 3 A). The 48 W rating applies at 12 V, not every source voltage. [1 mark]
(ii) Since useful heat = (3/4) × input energy, required electrical input = 4050/(3/4) = 5400 J. [1 mark]
Time = 5400/27 = 200 s = 3 min 20 s. The deadline is 240 s, so the proposal meets it with 40 s to spare. [1 mark]
(iii) Using 48 W would predict 5400/48 = 112.5 s. At 9 V that interval supplies only 27 × 112.5 = 3037.5 J electrically, or 2278.125 J usefully, below 4050 J. Power varies as V² for the stated fixed resistance; the printed rating is not constant-power regulation. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: At 9 V, actual input power P = 9²/3 = 27 W (current 3 A). The 48 W rating applies at 12 V, not every source voltage.
(ii) Since useful heat = (3/4) × input energy, required electrical input = 4050/(3/4) = 5400 J.
Time = 5400/27 = 200 s = 3 min 20 s. The deadline is 240 s, so the proposal meets it with 40 s to spare.

(iii) Using 48 W would predict 5400/48 = 112.5 s. At 9 V that interval supplies only 27 × 112.5 = 3037.5 J electrically, or 2278.125 J usefully, below 4050 J. Power varies as V² for the stated fixed resistance; the printed rating is not constant-power regulation.

questions.competency_rationale: Resistance, altered-voltage power, and inversion of the explicitly supplied useful fraction are foundational. The deadline decision earns 1 and the quantitative diagnosis of the misused rating earns 1.

questions.text:
The figure shows the complete input-power schedule for a controlled resistive device during 0–60 s. The sloping segments are straight. The source can deliver at most 15 kJ during this run and at most 450 W at any instant. Use rectangles and triangles only; the energy of a straight ramp is its average endpoint power multiplied by its duration.
(i) Calculate the energy used in each of the three plotted intervals and the total. [2 marks]
(ii) Decide whether the plotted run satisfies both source limits, with evidence. [1 mark]
(iii) If the original plotted schedule is followed without modification, at what time does the accumulated energy first reach 9 kJ? Show how you locate the time. [2 marks]
questions.answer:
(i) From 0–20 s the triangular region gives (1/2) × 20 × 400 = 4000 J. From 20–40 s the rectangle gives 20 × 400 = 8000 J. Award 0.5 each. [1 mark]
From 40–60 s the trapezium gives [(400 + 200)/2] × 20 = 6000 J. Total = 4000 + 8000 + 6000 = 18000 J = 18 kJ. Award 0.5 each for the final interval and total. [1 mark]
(ii) Peak power is 400 W, below 450 W, so the power limit is satisfied. Total energy 18 kJ exceeds 15 kJ by 3 kJ, so the full run is not feasible within the energy limit. Award 0.5 for each test. [1 mark]
(iii) At 20 s, accumulated energy is 4 kJ; at 40 s it is 12 kJ. Thus 9 kJ is first reached during the constant 400 W interval, not on either ramp. [1 mark]
An additional 9000 − 4000 = 5000 J takes 5000/400 = 12.5 s after 20 s. The time from the start is therefore 32.5 s. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) From 0–20 s the triangular region gives (1/2) × 20 × 400 = 4000 J. From 20–40 s the rectangle gives 20 × 400 = 8000 J. Award 0.5 each.
From 40–60 s the trapezium gives [(400 + 200)/2] × 20 = 6000 J. Total = 4000 + 8000 + 6000 = 18000 J = 18 kJ. Award 0.5 each for the final interval and total.
(ii) Peak power is 400 W, below 450 W, so the power limit is satisfied. Total energy 18 kJ exceeds 15 kJ by 3 kJ, so the full run is not feasible within the energy limit. Award 0.5 for each test.
(iii) At 20 s, accumulated energy is 4 kJ; at 40 s it is 12 kJ. Thus 9 kJ is first reached during the constant 400 W interval, not on either ramp.
An additional 9000 − 4000 = 5000 J takes 5000/400 = 12.5 s after 20 s. The time from the start is therefore 32.5 s.

questions.competency_rationale: Requires decomposing a supplied graph, testing independent limits and locating a cumulative-energy threshold inside an interval. No slope differentiation or integration is used.

diagram_image.alt: Input-power graph with a rising ramp, a plateau and a falling ramp, over sixty seconds.

questions.text:
A field recorder has a source that maintains 6 V and can deliver 1800 J of electrical energy before stopping. Each complete recording cycle draws 0.30 A for 20 s, then 0.05 A for 100 s. There is no off-cycle consumption and no loss between source and recorder; each stated current is constant. A logbook says that “the battery has 300 coulombs of electrons which the recorder will destroy”.
(i) Find the charge passing through the recorder in one cycle. [1 mark]
(ii) Determine the maximum number of complete cycles the energy supply permits, including the energy left after those complete cycles. [2 marks]
(iii) Correct the logbook’s physical interpretation while explaining the origin of the number 300 C. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Case: charge, energy and cycle budget
questions.answer:
(i) Qcycle = 0.30 × 20 + 0.05 × 100 = 6 + 5 = 11 C. [1 mark]
(ii) Ecycle = VQ = 6 × 11 = 66 J. Since 1800/66 = 27.27…, only 27 complete cycles are possible; a fractional cycle does not count. [1 mark]
Energy used = 27 × 66 = 1782 J, leaving 18 J. A 28th full cycle needs 66 J, so the remainder is insufficient. [1 mark]
(iii) 1800 J/6 J per C = 300 C is the total charge that can pass through the external circuit under this fixed-voltage energy model. Electrons are not destroyed; the source transfers stored energy as charge circulates. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Ecycle = VQ = 6 × 11 = 66 J. Since 1800/66 = 27.27…, only 27 complete cycles are possible; a fractional cycle does not count.
Energy used = 27 × 66 = 1782 J, leaving 18 J. A 28th full cycle needs 66 J, so the remainder is insufficient.

(iii) 1800 J/6 J per C = 300 C is the total charge that can pass through the external circuit under this fixed-voltage energy model. Electrons are not destroyed; the source transfers stored energy as charge circulates.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is routine. The remaining marks require a whole-cycle decision and a distinction between deliverable charge-throughput and charge destruction.

questions.text:
A laboratory compares fixed resistors A = 4 Ω and B = 16 Ω. During each 30 s test all electrical energy is measured as generated heat. In session 1 the source is adjusted separately so that each resistor carries 0.50 A. In session 2 each resistor is connected separately to the same ideal 8 V source. A report merges the sessions and concludes: “Greater resistance always generates more heat.” No temperature-rise comparisons are requested.
(i) Find HA:HB in session 1 and the heat in B. [1 mark]
(ii) A student’s session-2 log records HA = 120 J and HB = 480 J. Diagnose this log using the predicted heat ratio, and give the corrected heat in A. [1 mark]
(iii) Rewrite the report’s conclusion so that it is valid for both sessions, explaining the different control variables. [1 mark]
(iv) A third session doubles both A’s current and its test duration relative to session 1. The measured heat is eight times its session-1 value. A student concludes that doubling current alone causes eight times the heat. Evaluate this conclusion and specify a repeat that isolates the current effect, including the expected heat factor. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Case: evidence under different electrical controls
questions.answer:
(i) At equal I and t, HA:HB = RA:RB = 4:16 = 1:4. HB = 0.50² × 16 × 30 = 120 J. Award 0.5 each. [1 mark]
(ii) At equal V and t, HA:HB = RB:RA = 16:4 = 4:1, not the logged 1:4. HA = 8² × 30/4 = 480 J and HB = 8² × 30/16 = 120 J: the entries are interchanged. Award 0.5 for diagnosing the reversed allocation using the ratio and 0.5 for the corrected 480 J with working. [1 mark]
(iii) At fixed current and time, larger resistance generates more heat; at fixed voltage and time, larger resistance generates less heat because the current decreases. The sessions cannot be merged into an unconditional rule about resistance. [1 mark]
(iv) The eightfold result is consistent with H ∝ I²t: doubling current gives factor 4 and doubling duration gives factor 2, together 8 (30 J becomes 240 J). It does not isolate current because duration also changed. Repeat with A at 1.0 A for the original 30 s, keeping resistance unchanged; expected heat is four times the original, 120 J. Award 0.5 for identifying the time confounder and 0.5 for the controlled repeat and factor 4. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) At equal I and t, HA:HB = RA:RB = 4:16 = 1:4. HB = 0.50² × 16 × 30 = 120 J. Award 0.5 each.

(ii) At equal V and t, HA:HB = RB:RA = 16:4 = 4:1, not the logged 1:4. HA = 8² × 30/4 = 480 J and HB = 8² × 30/16 = 120 J: the entries are interchanged. Award 0.5 for diagnosing the reversed allocation using the ratio and 0.5 for the corrected 480 J with working.

(iii) At fixed current and time, larger resistance generates more heat; at fixed voltage and time, larger resistance generates less heat because the current decreases. The sessions cannot be merged into an unconditional rule about resistance.

(iv) The eightfold result is consistent with H ∝ I²t: doubling current gives factor 4 and doubling duration gives factor 2, together 8 (30 J becomes 240 J). It does not isolate current because duration also changed. Repeat with A at 1.0 A for the original 30 s, keeping resistance unchanged; expected heat is four times the original, 120 J. Award 0.5 for identifying the time confounder and 0.5 for the controlled repeat and factor 4.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is routine (0). Part (ii) diagnoses a reversed data log against fixed-voltage predictions (1); part (iii) qualifies an invalid universal claim (1); part (iv) identifies a time confounder and designs a current-only repeat (1).

questions.text:
A team needs a fixed-resistance element to generate exactly 1800 J in 60 s when connected directly to an ideal 12 V source. All input energy becomes generated heat. Three uniform candidate wires of the same stable alloy and temperature are available: A has length 0.50 m and area 0.10 mm²; B has length 1.00 m and area 0.20 mm²; C has length 0.50 m and area 0.20 mm². The alloy resistivity is 9.6 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. The wires are alternatives, not connected together.
(i) Determine the required resistance from the task. [1 mark]
(ii) Calculate the three candidate resistances and choose all candidates that meet the task exactly. [2 marks]
(iii) A student says B must be rejected because it is longer than A. Explain why that reasoning is incomplete. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Case: material geometry and heat specification
questions.answer:
(i) Required power = 1800/60 = 30 W. Required resistance = V²/P = 12²/30 = 4.8 Ω. [1 mark]
(ii) Using 0.10 mm² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m² and 0.20 mm² = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ m², RA = (9.6 × 10⁻⁷ × 0.50)/(1.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 4.8 Ω; RB = (9.6 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.00)/(2.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 4.8 Ω; RC = 2.4 Ω. Award 1 mark for all three. [1 mark]
A and B both meet the 4.8 Ω target and each generates 1800 J in 60 s. C generates 12² × 60/2.4 = 3600 J, twice the target, so it does not meet the exact specification. [1 mark]
(iii) B has twice A’s length but also twice its cross-sectional area; the two effects cancel in R = ρL/A. Length alone cannot rank their resistances or heating at fixed voltage. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Required power = 1800/60 = 30 W. Required resistance = V²/P = 12²/30 = 4.8 Ω.
A and B both meet the 4.8 Ω target and each generates 1800 J in 60 s. C generates 12² × 60/2.4 = 3600 J, twice the target, so it does not meet the exact specification.
(iii) B has twice A’s length but also twice its cross-sectional area; the two effects cancel in R = ρL/A. Length alone cannot rank their resistances or heating at fixed voltage.

questions.competency_rationale: Required resistance and three direct geometry substitutions are foundational. Selecting all compliant candidates with a heat check earns 1; explaining cancellation of length and area effects earns 1.

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes electric current and the connection of an ammeter used to measure the current through a resistor? [1 mark]
options: Current is energy transferred each second; connect the ammeter in series.
Current is charge passing a cross-section each second; connect the ammeter in series.
Current is charge passing a cross-section each second; connect the ammeter in parallel.
Current is energy transferred per coulomb; connect the ammeter in parallel.
questions.answer: B. Current is the rate of flow of charge across a cross-section. An ammeter is connected in series with the resistor so that the current being measured passes through the meter. The other choices confuse current with energy or voltage, or put the ammeter across the resistor. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: B. Current is the rate of flow of charge across a cross-section. An ammeter is connected in series with the resistor so that the current being measured passes through the meter. The other choices confuse current with energy or voltage, or put the ammeter across the resistor.

questions.competency_rationale: Recall of the definition of current and the standard ammeter connection; no charge-time calculation or competency claim.
ncert_refs: NCERT Ch.11 §11.1, printed pp.171–172: current and ammeter connection.

questions.text: Take V and Q as positive. In trial X, a source transfers energy W while moving charge Q through a potential difference V. In trial Y, the potential difference is 3V and the transferred charge is Q/2. What is the electrical work done in trial Y? [1 mark]
questions.topic: Work from voltage and charge ratios
questions.answer: C. Electrical work is voltage multiplied by charge. Thus W_Y = (3V)(Q/2) = (3/2)VQ = 3W/2. Multiplying the voltage ratio 3 by the charge ratio 1/2 gives 3/2, not 6 or 1/6. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: C. Electrical work is voltage multiplied by charge. Thus W_Y = (3V)(Q/2) = (3/2)VQ = 3W/2. Multiplying the voltage ratio 3 by the charge ratio 1/2 gives 3/2, not 6 or 1/6.

questions.competency_rationale: A direct two-factor W = VQ ratio comparison, conservatively foundational; not a repeat of computing voltage from a supplied work/charge pair.
ncert_refs: NCERT Ch.11 §11.2, printed pp.173–174: V = W/Q and W = VQ.

questions.text: The figure gives measured I–V lines for wires P and Q at the same temperature. P has length L and conducting area A; Q has length 4L and conducting area A. Which material-resistivity relation is supported after allowing for this unequal geometry? [1 mark]
options: P has twice the resistivity of Q.
Q has twice the resistivity of P.
They have equal resistivity because their areas are equal.
Q has four times the resistivity of P.
questions.answer: A. At 4 V the graph gives I_P = 0.8 A and I_Q = 0.4 A, so R_P = 5 Ω and R_Q = 10 Ω. Resistivity is RA/L, hence ρ_Q/ρ_P = (10/5)(A/A)(L/4L) = 1/2. Thus P has twice Q’s resistivity even though P has the smaller measured resistance. Ignoring the fourfold length would reverse this material ranking; slope on these axes is I/V, not R. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: A. At 4 V the graph gives I_P = 0.8 A and I_Q = 0.4 A, so R_P = 5 Ω and R_Q = 10 Ω. Resistivity is RA/L, hence ρ_Q/ρ_P = (10/5)(A/A)(L/4L) = 1/2. Thus P has twice Q’s resistivity even though P has the smaller measured resistance. Ignoring the fourfold length would reverse this material ranking; slope on these axes is I/V, not R.

questions.competency_rationale: Reads the I-vertical graph, then removes the known length difference to reverse the apparent resistance-based material ranking. Equal-geometry comparison is no longer available.
ncert_refs: NCERT Ch.11 §11.4, Activity 11.1, printed pp.175–176: V/I and graph interpretation.
NCERT Ch.11 §11.5, Activity 11.3, printed pp.177–179: R proportional to length, inverse area and material resistivity.

diagram_image.alt: Measured current–voltage lines for wires P and Q; axes and readings shown.

questions.text: A uniform sample X has length L and area A. Sample Y has length 2L and area 2A. At the same temperature both have resistance 8 Ω. Which conclusion follows? [1 mark]
options: Y has half the resistivity of X.
Y has twice the resistivity of X.
The two samples have equal resistivity, but this alone does not prove identical composition.
Equal resistance proves identical chemical composition.
questions.answer: C. ρ = RA/L. For Y, the factors of 2 in area and length cancel; both give ρ = 8A/L. Equal resistivity is not a unique chemical identification. [1 mark for the correct option.]

marking_scheme.step: Select C; ρ = RA/L. For Y, the factors of 2 in area and length cancel; both give ρ = 8A/L. Equal resistivity is not a unique chemical identification.

questions.competency_rationale: Separates a measurable electrical property from an unsupported identity claim after controlling the geometry ratio.
ncert_refs: NCERT Class X Science, Ch.11 §11.5, Activity 11.3, printed pp.177–179; Example 11.6, p.180

questions.text: A cable maker doubles only the outer diameter of the plastic insulation around a metal core. Core material, core diameter and core length stay unchanged. Which statement about the resistance between the core ends is correct? [1 mark]
options: It is unchanged because the conducting cross-section is unchanged.
It becomes one-quarter because the outer diameter doubles.
It becomes one-half because insulation is thicker.
It doubles because the cable is wider.
questions.answer: A. R = ρL/A uses the conducting metal area, not the area enclosed by the insulation. None of ρ, L or conducting A changes. [1 mark for the correct option.]

marking_scheme.step: Select A; R = ρL/A uses the conducting metal area, not the area enclosed by the insulation. None of ρ, L or conducting A changes.

questions.competency_rationale: Discriminates conducting diameter from an irrelevant outer geometric measurement.

questions.text: The circuit in the figure is connected to an ideal 9 V source. Which pair gives the source current and the current through the upper 6 Ω resistor, respectively? [1 mark]
questions.answer: D. The two 6 Ω resistors share the same two nodes, so their parallel equivalent is 3 Ω. With the 3 Ω series resistor, R_total = 6 Ω and I_source = 9/6 = 1.5 A. Identical parallel branches divide this equally: 0.75 A each. [1 mark for the correct option.]

marking_scheme.step: Select D; The two 6 Ω resistors share the same two nodes, so their parallel equivalent is 3 Ω. With the 3 Ω series resistor, R_total = 6 Ω and I_source = 9/6 = 1.5 A. Identical parallel branches divide this equally: 0.75 A each.

questions.competency_rationale: Requires extracting series/parallel connectivity from node dots, then distinguishing source and branch currents.

questions.text: In a steady series circuit, 18 C passes into a heater in 6 s. A student says that only 12 C will leave it in those 6 s because the rest becomes heat. Which correction is valid? [1 mark]
options: 12 C leaves, but the lost charge becomes light rather than heat.
18 C leaves; electrical energy is transferred but charge is not consumed.
36 C leaves because electrons multiply in a hot wire.
questions.answer: B. The steady current is the same on both sides: I = 18/6 = 3 A. Thus 18 C also leaves in 6 s. Heating transfers energy, not charge into heat. [1 mark for the correct option.]

marking_scheme.step: Select B; The steady current is the same on both sides: I = 18/6 = 3 A. Thus 18 C also leaves in 6 s. Heating transfers energy, not charge into heat.

questions.text: A wire has conducting cross-sectional area 0.35 mm². Express this area in m² for use in R = ρL/A. [1 mark]
questions.answer: C. Since 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m². Therefore 0.35 mm² = 0.35×10⁻⁶ m² = 3.5×10⁻⁷ m². The conversion factor must be squared because the quantity is an area. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: C. Since 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m². Therefore 0.35 mm² = 0.35×10⁻⁶ m² = 3.5×10⁻⁷ m². The conversion factor must be squared because the quantity is an area.

questions.competency_rationale: Direct area-unit conversion; foundational rather than material inference or resistivity-unit recall.

questions.text: A class records (V, I) as (1.2 V, 0.20 A), (2.4 V, 0.40 A), (3.6 V, 0.60 A) and (4.8 V, 0.60 A). A repeat at 4.8 V gives 0.80 A. Which claim is best supported? [1 mark]
options: The repeat restores the common 6 Ω pattern; the first last-row reading should be investigated.
Every reading proves resistance is 8 Ω.
One discrepant reading proves that all metal wires disobey Ohm’s law.
questions.answer: A. The first three ratios V/I equal 6 Ω; the original final row gives 8 Ω, while the repeat gives 6 Ω. The repeat supports investigating the outlier, not declaring a universal failure or silently discarding data. [1 mark for the correct option.]

marking_scheme.step: Select A; The first three ratios V/I equal 6 Ω; the original final row gives 8 Ω, while the repeat gives 6 Ω. The repeat supports investigating the outlier, not declaring a universal failure or silently discarding data.

questions.competency_rationale: Compares a repeated observation with a consistent model and limits the conclusion.

questions.answer: D. At fixed ρ and L, R ∝ 1/A and A ∝ d². Doubling d gives four times the area and one-quarter the resistance: 1 Ω. [1 mark for the correct option.]

questions.text: Two coils have resistances 4 Ω and 8 Ω. A student states, “The 8 Ω coil always produces more heat in one minute.” All currents and applied voltages in the choices are nonzero. Which test condition makes this claim false? [1 mark]
options: The same current is maintained in both coils.
Each coil is connected separately across the same ideal voltage.
Both carry 1 A for one minute.
The same charge crosses each in one minute at steady current.
questions.answer: B. At equal voltage and equal time, H = V²t/R, so the 8 Ω coil produces half the heat of the 4 Ω coil. The other choices imply equal current and time, when H = I²Rt gives more heat in 8 Ω. [1 mark for the correct option.]

marking_scheme.step: Select B; At equal voltage and equal time, H = V²t/R, so the 8 Ω coil produces half the heat of the 4 Ω coil. The other choices imply equal current and time, when H = I²Rt gives more heat in 8 Ω.

questions.competency_rationale: Identifies the controlled variable that reverses a heating comparison.

questions.text: Two identical uniform wires each have length L and resistance R. Design E cuts one wire into two equal pieces and connects those pieces in parallel. Design U cuts the other wire into lengths L/4 and 3L/4 and connects those pieces in parallel. Both designs use the entire wire, with negligible cutting loss, and are tested separately across the same nonzero ideal voltage. Which design draws more source current? [1 mark]
options: U, because its equivalent resistance is 3R/16, smaller than E’s R/4.
E, because equal branches always draw more total current.
Both draw the same current because the total wire length is equal.
U, because its equivalent resistance is 3R/4, larger than E’s R/4.
questions.answer: A. E has two R/2 pieces in parallel, giving R_E = R/4. U has R/4 and 3R/4 in parallel, giving R_U = (R/4)(3R/4)/R = 3R/16. At the same voltage, I_U/I_E = R_E/R_U = 4/3, so U draws more source current. Equal total length does not fix equivalent resistance after reconnection. [1 mark for the correct option.]

marking_scheme.step: A. E has two R/2 pieces in parallel, giving R_E = R/4. U has R/4 and 3R/4 in parallel, giving R_U = (R/4)(3R/4)/R = 3R/16. At the same voltage, I_U/I_E = R_E/R_U = 4/3, so U draws more source current. Equal total length does not fix equivalent resistance after reconnection. [1 mark for the correct option.]

questions.competency_rationale: Compares equal and unequal material allocations in parallel and rejects the inference that equal total length fixes source current.

Only the maximum current rating of the source.
The conducting cross-sectional area of each sample.
questions.answer: D. Measure each conducting area, then use ρ = RA/L at the same temperature. Larger R alone cannot rank material resistivity when A differs. [1 mark for the correct option.]

The same end-to-end resistance, because material, path length and cross-section are unchanged.
Zero resistance because turns are close together.

questions.text:
A sample is known to be one of three chemically different candidate materials K, M or N. At the test temperature, K and M each have resistivity 8.0×10⁻⁷ Ω m, while N has resistivity 1.2×10⁻⁶ Ω m. The sample’s resistivity is measured exactly as 8.0×10⁻⁷ Ω m.
Assertion (A): This measurement rules out N and uniquely identifies the sample as K.
Reason (R): The supplied candidate data include two chemically different materials with the same resistivity at the test temperature. [1 mark]
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.answer: D. A is false: the measurement excludes N but cannot distinguish K from M, so it does not uniquely identify K. R is true: the stated K and M values are equal despite their different compositions. A matching resistivity can leave more than one candidate; an unequal value at the controlled temperature can exclude a candidate. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: D. A is false: the measurement excludes N but cannot distinguish K from M, so it does not uniquely identify K. R is true: the stated K and M values are equal despite their different compositions. A matching resistivity can leave more than one candidate; an unequal value at the controlled temperature can exclude a candidate.

questions.competency_rationale: Uses explicit candidate evidence to distinguish exclusion from unique identification; no stretch-factor calculation or rehearsal of the conserved-volume long task.

Assertion (A): For wires of equal material and length, doubling the conducting diameter halves the resistance.
Reason (R): The conducting cross-sectional area is proportional to the square of the diameter. [1 mark]
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.

questions.answer: D. A is false: doubling diameter multiplies area by four and reduces resistance to one-quarter, not one-half. R is true and identifies the missed squared relationship. [1 mark for the correct option.]

questions.text:
Assertion (A): Connecting a second positive, finite resistance in parallel with a resistor across an ideal fixed-voltage source increases the source current.
Reason (R): The voltage across the original resistor increases when the branch is added. [1 mark]
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not correctly explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.answer: C. A is true: the new branch draws additional current while the original branch current remains V/R. R is false because the ideal source maintains the same voltage across both branches. [1 mark for the correct option.]

questions.text:
Two conductors are tested separately. In X, 72 C crosses a section in 3 minutes. In Y, 90 C crosses a section in 5 minutes.
(i) Calculate both average currents. [1 mark]
(ii) A learner ranks Y as having the larger current because more charge passed through it. Correct the ranking with a reason. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) I_X = 72/180 = 0.40 A and I_Y = 90/300 = 0.30 A (0.5 mark each). [1 mark]
(ii) X has the larger average current. Current compares charge per unit time, not total charge measured over different times. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) X has the larger average current. Current compares charge per unit time, not total charge measured over different times.

questions.competency_rationale: Only part (ii) evaluates an invalid comparison; part (i) is routine substitution.

questions.text:
Two sources deliver equal electrical energy, 180 J each, to resistors. Source U moves 30 C; source V moves 15 C.
(i) Determine which source has greater potential difference and by what factor. [1 mark]
(ii) Will equal amounts of charge receive equal energy from these two sources? Justify. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) V_U = 180/30 = 6 V; V_V = 180/15 = 12 V. Source V has twice the potential difference despite equal total energy delivered in the stated trials. [1 mark]
(ii) No. W = VQ, so for any same nonzero charge Q, source V transfers twice the energy transferred by U. Equal trial energies arose from different charges. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) V_U = 180/30 = 6 V; V_V = 180/15 = 12 V. Source V has twice the potential difference despite equal total energy delivered in the stated trials.
(ii) No. W = VQ, so for any same nonzero charge Q, source V transfers twice the energy transferred by U. Equal trial energies arose from different charges.

questions.competency_rationale: Only (ii) transfers the result to an equal-charge comparison; (i) is direct division and ratio.

questions.text:
A technician intends to measure only the resistance of wire X. The supplied diagram shows the actual meter connections. The ammeter reads 0.30 A and the voltmeter reads 3.0 V.
(i) Explain why using 3.0/0.30 does not give the resistance of X, and state the correct terminals for the voltmeter. [1 mark]
(ii) Find the resistance of X using the diagram and readings. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) The voltmeter spans M to P, including X and the 4 Ω resistor. It should span M to N to measure X alone; its present reading divided by current is the combined resistance. [1 mark]
(ii) R_MP = 3.0/0.30 = 10 Ω. Since the same current passes through X and 4 Ω, R_X = 10 − 4 = 6 Ω. Equivalently V_X = 3.0 − 0.30×4 = 1.8 V and R_X = 1.8/0.30 = 6 Ω. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) The voltmeter spans M to P, including X and the 4 Ω resistor. It should span M to N to measure X alone; its present reading divided by current is the combined resistance.
(ii) R_MP = 3.0/0.30 = 10 Ω. Since the same current passes through X and 4 Ω, R_X = 10 − 4 = 6 Ω. Equivalently V_X = 3.0 − 0.30×4 = 1.8 V and R_X = 1.8/0.30 = 6 Ω.

questions.competency_rationale: Both marks require diagnosing the actual instrument span, not merely substituting nominal meter readings.

questions.text:
For a uniform conductor, write the relation connecting resistance R, resistivity ρ, length L and conducting cross-sectional area A.
(i) Use it to express ρ. [1 mark]
(ii) State what physical property ρ describes and its SI unit. [1 mark]

(ii) Resistivity characterises the material’s opposition to current independently of the specimen dimensions at a specified temperature (0.5). Its SI unit is Ω m (0.5). [1 mark]
