questions.text:
A constant 0.50 A flows through an 8 Ω resistor for 120 s.
(i) Calculate the heat generated. [1 mark]
(ii) The current is doubled but the operating time is halved. Without assuming unchanged voltage, determine the new heat and explain the factor of change. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) H = I²Rt = (0.50)²×8×120 = 240 J. [1 mark]
(ii) H′/H = (2I)²(R)(t/2)/(I²Rt) = 2, so H′ = 480 J. Squaring the current gives a factor of four, then halving time gives an overall factor of two. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) H′/H = (2I)²(R)(t/2)/(I²Rt) = 2, so H′ = 480 J. Squaring the current gives a factor of four, then halving time gives an overall factor of two.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (ii) reasons across two changed variables; part (i) is foundational calculation.

questions.text:
In this test only, the wire temperature is allowed to change. A uniform wire draws 0.40 A at 2.0 V when cool and 0.32 A at 2.0 V after warming. Treat its length and conducting area as unchanged.
(i) Find the ratio of its warm resistivity to its cool resistivity. [1 mark]
(ii) A learner says the rise in resistance proves that the wire has become a different material. Explain why this is not established, and propose a useful repeat measurement. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) R_cool = 2.0/0.40 = 5.0 Ω and R_warm = 2.0/0.32 = 6.25 Ω. Since L and A are unchanged, ρ_warm/ρ_cool = R_warm/R_cool = 6.25/5.0 = 1.25. [1 mark]
(ii) Resistivity can vary with temperature even without a change in material, so the two-temperature comparison does not establish a new composition (0.5 mark). Cool the wire back to the original temperature and repeat the same-voltage measurement; recovery of the original current would support a reversible temperature effect (0.5 mark). [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) R_cool = 2.0/0.40 = 5.0 Ω and R_warm = 2.0/0.32 = 6.25 Ω. Since L and A are unchanged, ρ_warm/ρ_cool = R_warm/R_cool = 6.25/5.0 = 1.25.

(ii) Resistivity can vary with temperature even without a change in material, so the two-temperature comparison does not establish a new composition (0.5 mark). Cool the wire back to the original temperature and repeat the same-voltage measurement; recovery of the original current would support a reversible temperature effect (0.5 mark).

questions.competency_rationale: Only (ii) diagnoses temperature confounding and proposes a repeat; (i) is routine ratio calculation.

questions.text:
The diagram gives measured resistances and dimensions of three uniform samples P, Q and T at one temperature.
(i) Which pair has equal resistivity? Show a comparison using the labelled values. [1 mark]
(ii) Find ρ_T/ρ_P. [1 mark]
(iii) A student says, “Q must be made of the highest-resistivity material because it has the greatest resistance.” Explain the error using this evidence. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) Compare RA/L in common units. P gives 4×0.50/1.0 = 2 and Q gives 8×0.50/2.0 = 2 in Ω mm²/m; hence P and Q have equal resistivity (2×10⁻⁶ Ω m). [1 mark]
(ii) T gives 4×1.00/1.0 = 4 in the same units. Thus ρ_T/ρ_P = 4/2 = 2. [1 mark]
(iii) Q’s higher resistance than P is explained by its doubled length, not by higher resistivity. T has the greatest resistivity even though its measured resistance equals P’s, because T has twice P’s area at the same length. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Compare RA/L in common units. P gives 4×0.50/1.0 = 2 and Q gives 8×0.50/2.0 = 2 in Ω mm²/m; hence P and Q have equal resistivity (2×10⁻⁶ Ω m).
(ii) T gives 4×1.00/1.0 = 4 in the same units. Thus ρ_T/ρ_P = 4/2 = 2.

(iii) Q’s higher resistance than P is explained by its doubled length, not by higher resistivity. T has the greatest resistivity even though its measured resistance equals P’s, because T has twice P’s area at the same length.

questions.competency_rationale: Count (i) geometry-normalised pair selection and (iii) diagnosis; (ii) is a routine ratio from computed values.

questions.text:
A spool is sampled at the same temperature and conducting area. At 2.0 V, lengths 0.50 m, 1.00 m and 2.00 m draw 0.40 A, 0.20 A and 0.10 A respectively.
(i) Calculate R/L for all three samples and state whether they support a common resistance-per-length model. [1 mark]
(ii) A sensor test requires current from 0.12 A to 0.15 A inclusive at 2.0 V. Choose a length from 1.0 m, 1.5 m and 2.0 m, showing why the others fail. [2 marks]
questions.topic: Length evidence for a current target
questions.answer:
(i) Resistances are 5, 10 and 20 Ω, respectively. Dividing by 0.50, 1.00 and 2.00 m gives 10 Ω/m in every case, supporting R = (10 Ω/m)L for this spool under the test conditions. [1 mark]
(ii) The three candidate resistances are 10, 15 and 20 Ω. Their currents are 0.20 A, 2/15 A ≈ 0.133 A and 0.10 A (1 mark). Choose 1.5 m: only 0.133 A is within 0.12–0.15 A; 1.0 m draws too much and 2.0 m too little (1 mark). [2 marks]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Resistances are 5, 10 and 20 Ω, respectively. Dividing by 0.50, 1.00 and 2.00 m gives 10 Ω/m in every case, supporting R = (10 Ω/m)L for this spool under the test conditions.

(ii) The three candidate resistances are 10, 15 and 20 Ω. Their currents are 0.20 A, 2/15 A ≈ 0.133 A and 0.10 A (1 mark). Choose 1.5 m: only 0.133 A is within 0.12–0.15 A; 1.0 m draws too much and 2.0 m too little (1 mark).

questions.competency_rationale: Count (i) model consistency and the one-mark admissibility decision in (ii); candidate-current calculations are foundational.

questions.text:
Two unknown resistors X and Y are in series across 6.0 V. The steady current is 0.50 A; the measured voltage across X is 2.0 V.
(i) Find the resistance of X. [1 mark]
(ii) Infer the voltage and resistance of Y. [1 mark]
(iii) A student predicts equal heat in X and Y over the same time because their currents are equal. Evaluate this prediction. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) R_X = V_X/I = 2.0/0.50 = 4.0 Ω. [1 mark]
(ii) Series voltages add, so V_Y = 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 V. R_Y = 4.0/0.50 = 8.0 Ω. [1 mark]
(iii) The prediction is false. At common current and time, H = I²Rt, so H_Y/H_X = 8/4 = 2; Y generates twice the heat. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Series voltages add, so V_Y = 6.0 − 2.0 = 4.0 V. R_Y = 4.0/0.50 = 8.0 Ω.
(iii) The prediction is false. At common current and time, H = I²Rt, so H_Y/H_X = 8/4 = 2; Y generates twice the heat.

questions.competency_rationale: Only (iii) challenges a heat misconception; routine series-voltage subtraction and Ohm-law calculation in (i)–(ii) are foundational.

questions.text:
A single continuous wire has two uniform sections made of the same material, joined end to end with no branch and negligible junction resistance. Section X is 0.40 m long with area 0.20 mm²; section Y is 0.80 m long with area 0.40 mm². The operating resistivity of both is 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m and is treated as constant. For part (iii), override the general constant-temperature and neglected-loss assumptions: initial temperatures and heat-loss conditions are unspecified, and temperatures may change. Continue to treat the stated electrical resistivity as constant; no thermal calculation is required. A steady current of 0.50 A flows through the wire for 40 s.
(i) Find the resistance and total heat generated in each section. [1 mark]
(ii) Power generated per metre means a section’s electrical power divided by its length. A designer wants the larger heat-generation rate per metre. Choose X or Y and justify numerically, explaining why the current is not smaller in the narrower section. [1 mark]
(iii) A learner claims that your choice in (ii) must reach the higher temperature. Is that conclusion established by these electrical data alone? Explain without using a temperature-rise formula. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Localising heating in a nonuniform single wire
questions.answer:
(i) A_X = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m² and A_Y = 4.0×10⁻⁷ m². R_X = 1.0×10⁻⁶×0.40/(2.0×10⁻⁷) = 2.0 Ω and R_Y = 1.0×10⁻⁶×0.80/(4.0×10⁻⁷) = 2.0 Ω (0.5 mark for both resistances). Each generates H = (0.50)²×2.0×40 = 20 J (0.5 mark for both heats). [1 mark]
(ii) There is one steady unbranched path, so the current is 0.50 A in both sections; charge does not disappear or accumulate at the narrowing. Each generates P = I²R = 0.50 W, but P_X/L_X = 0.50/0.40 = 1.25 W/m and P_Y/L_Y = 0.50/0.80 = 0.625 W/m. Choose X: it has twice the heat-generation rate per metre, although the sections generate equal total heat. [1 mark]
(iii) No. A larger electrical heat-generation rate per metre does not by itself determine the temperature attained. Heat loss/cooling and the amount of material being warmed also matter. Those thermal conditions are not specified; the calculation establishes generated energy and power per metre, not a temperature ranking. No temperature change in resistivity is used in this model. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) A_X = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m² and A_Y = 4.0×10⁻⁷ m². R_X = 1.0×10⁻⁶×0.40/(2.0×10⁻⁷) = 2.0 Ω and R_Y = 1.0×10⁻⁶×0.80/(4.0×10⁻⁷) = 2.0 Ω (0.5 mark for both resistances). Each generates H = (0.50)²×2.0×40 = 20 J (0.5 mark for both heats).

(ii) There is one steady unbranched path, so the current is 0.50 A in both sections; charge does not disappear or accumulate at the narrowing. Each generates P = I²R = 0.50 W, but P_X/L_X = 0.50/0.40 = 1.25 W/m and P_Y/L_Y = 0.50/0.80 = 0.625 W/m. Choose X: it has twice the heat-generation rate per metre, although the sections generate equal total heat.

(iii) No. A larger electrical heat-generation rate per metre does not by itself determine the temperature attained. Heat loss/cooling and the amount of material being warmed also matter. Those thermal conditions are not specified; the calculation establishes generated energy and power per metre, not a temperature ranking. No temperature change in resistivity is used in this model.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is routine resistance/heating arithmetic. Count the spatial heat-localisation decision and common-current explanation in (ii), plus the limit of the temperature inference in (iii).

questions.text:
The plotted lines show resistance against length for two uniform wire stocks. Stock X has conducting area 0.50 mm²; stock Y has conducting area 0.25 mm².
(i) Read each resistance-per-metre value from the graph. [1 mark]
(ii) Compare their resistivities. [1 mark]
(iii) A 6 Ω resistor must fit a path of at most 2.0 m. It must be a single piece with the stock area unchanged. Which stock can meet this requirement, and what length should be cut? [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) At 2 m the graph gives 4 Ω for X and 8 Ω for Y. Thus R/L is 2 Ω/m for X and 4 Ω/m for Y. [1 mark]
(ii) ρ = (R/L)A. For X, ρ_X = 2×0.50×10⁻⁶ = 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m. For Y, ρ_Y = 4×0.25×10⁻⁶ = 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m. The stocks have equal resistivity despite unequal graph slopes. [1 mark]
(iii) X requires L = 6/2 = 3 m, exceeding the limit. Y requires L = 6/4 = 1.5 m, which fits. Choose 1.5 m of Y. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) At 2 m the graph gives 4 Ω for X and 8 Ω for Y. Thus R/L is 2 Ω/m for X and 4 Ω/m for Y.
(ii) ρ = (R/L)A. For X, ρ_X = 2×0.50×10⁻⁶ = 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m. For Y, ρ_Y = 4×0.25×10⁻⁶ = 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m. The stocks have equal resistivity despite unequal graph slopes.
(iii) X requires L = 6/2 = 3 m, exceeding the limit. Y requires L = 6/4 = 1.5 m, which fits. Choose 1.5 m of Y.

questions.competency_rationale: Part (i) is a straightforward graph read-off, conservatively foundational. Parts (ii)–(iii) normalise geometry and apply a length constraint to choose stock.

questions.text:
A workshop’s cumulative electrical-energy meter reads 1250 kWh at the start of a billing period and 1268 kWh at its end. All the metered consumption occurred during a total of 30 energised hours; there was no consumption outside those hours. The tariff is ₹4 per kWh for the first 10 kWh consumed in this period and ₹7 per kWh for only the consumption above 10 kWh; ignore fixed charges and taxes. A proposed replacement is independently confirmed to give the same required useful output while reducing the period’s electrical consumption by 6 kWh.
(i) Find the consumed electrical energy and the average input power during the 30 energised hours. [1 mark]
(ii) Calculate the original bill using the stated tariff. [1 mark]
(iii) A manager predicts a saving of only ₹24 by pricing all 6 saved kWh at ₹4. Calculate the actual bill reduction and assess this prediction. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Meter readings and a tiered energy bill
questions.answer:
(i) Consumed energy is the increase in the cumulative reading: 1268 − 1250 = 18 kWh (0.5 mark). Average input power during energised hours = 18 kWh/30 h = 0.60 kW = 600 W (0.5 mark). [1 mark]
(ii) Only the first 10 kWh is charged at ₹4; the other 18 − 10 = 8 kWh is charged at ₹7. Original bill = 10×4 + 8×7 = ₹96. The cumulative meter total is not the period consumption, and the higher rate does not apply to all 18 kWh. [1 mark]
(iii) Replacement consumption = 18 − 6 = 12 kWh; new bill = 10×4 + 2×7 = ₹54. The bill falls by ₹96 − ₹54 = ₹42, not ₹24. Both totals exceed 10 kWh, so all six avoided kWh belong to the ₹7 tier. Equal required output is supplied as evidence, not inferred from power alone. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Consumed energy is the increase in the cumulative reading: 1268 − 1250 = 18 kWh (0.5 mark). Average input power during energised hours = 18 kWh/30 h = 0.60 kW = 600 W (0.5 mark).

(ii) Only the first 10 kWh is charged at ₹4; the other 18 − 10 = 8 kWh is charged at ₹7. Original bill = 10×4 + 8×7 = ₹96. The cumulative meter total is not the period consumption, and the higher rate does not apply to all 18 kWh.

(iii) Replacement consumption = 18 − 6 = 12 kWh; new bill = 10×4 + 2×7 = ₹54. The bill falls by ₹96 − ₹54 = ₹42, not ₹24. Both totals exceed 10 kWh, so all six avoided kWh belong to the ₹7 tier. Equal required output is supplied as evidence, not inferred from power alone.

questions.competency_rationale: Parts (i) and (ii) are foundational meter/power and explicitly specified tariff arithmetic. Count only (iii), which evaluates the manager’s wrong-tier claim against the changed total-consumption baseline.

questions.text:
A heater must have resistance 20 Ω, length 1.0 m and conducting area 0.050 mm². Three hypothetical materials are offered: K has resistivity 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m and withstands the operating temperature without rapid oxidation; L has resistivity 2.0×10⁻⁸ Ω m and also withstands it; M has resistivity 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m but rapidly oxidises at that temperature. Use the supplied operating resistivities.
(i) Determine which materials meet the electrical resistance requirement. [1 mark]
(ii) Choose the suitable material when durability is also required, and explain why each other material fails a requirement. [1 mark]
(iii) If the length of L stays 1.0 m, calculate the conducting area needed to reach 20 Ω and explain why this cannot satisfy the original fixed-geometry requirement. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) A = 0.050×10⁻⁶ = 5.0×10⁻⁸ m². R_K = R_M = 1.0×10⁻⁶/(5.0×10⁻⁸) = 20 Ω; R_L = 2.0×10⁻⁸/(5.0×10⁻⁸) = 0.40 Ω. K and M meet the electrical requirement. [1 mark]
(ii) Choose K. L fails the 20 Ω requirement at the specified geometry; M meets the resistance requirement but fails the oxidation/durability requirement. [1 mark]
(iii) A_L = ρ_L L/R = 2.0×10⁻⁸×1.0/20 = 1.0×10⁻⁹ m² = 0.0010 mm². This is only 1/50 of the required 0.050 mm², so it violates the fixed-area specification. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) A = 0.050×10⁻⁶ = 5.0×10⁻⁸ m². R_K = R_M = 1.0×10⁻⁶/(5.0×10⁻⁸) = 20 Ω; R_L = 2.0×10⁻⁸/(5.0×10⁻⁸) = 0.40 Ω. K and M meet the electrical requirement.
(ii) Choose K. L fails the 20 Ω requirement at the specified geometry; M meets the resistance requirement but fails the oxidation/durability requirement.
(iii) A_L = ρ_L L/R = 2.0×10⁻⁸×1.0/20 = 1.0×10⁻⁹ m² = 0.0010 mm². This is only 1/50 of the required 0.050 mm², so it violates the fixed-area specification.

questions.competency_rationale: Count (ii) joint electrical/durability screening and (iii) inadmissible-workaround assessment; (i) is routine candidate substitution.

questions.text:
A manufacturer has the original uniform wire shown in the figure. The full wire must be redrawn into one uniform wire, with no material removed or added and no change in resistivity. A 1.00 Ω component is required. It must also satisfy the maximum length and minimum conducting area stated on the drawing.
(i) Calculate the original conducting-material volume and explain the relation between the new area A′ and length L′. [1 mark]
(ii) Determine the length and area needed for 1.00 Ω, using conservation of volume rather than assuming fixed area. [2 marks]
(iii) Does the proposed wire satisfy both manufacturing limits? Show the checks. [1 mark]
(iv) Compare its power with that of the original wire when each is separately tested across 2.0 V. [1 mark]
questions.answer:
(i) Original volume = AL = 0.50 mm²×0.80 m = 0.40 mm² m = 4.0×10⁻⁷ m³. Conservation gives A′L′ = AL, or A′ = AL/L′. [1 mark]
(ii) Let k = L′/L. Then A′ = A/k, so R′/R = (L′/L)(A/A′) = k² (1 mark). Here 1.00/0.25 = 4, so k = 2 (positive length), L′ = 1.60 m and A′ = 0.25 mm² (1 mark). [2 marks]
(iii) The design is feasible: 1.60 m ≤ the 1.70 m maximum, and 0.25 mm² ≥ the 0.20 mm² minimum. Both conditions must hold. [1 mark]
(iv) At fixed 2.0 V, P_original = 2.0²/0.25 = 16 W; P_new = 2.0²/1.00 = 4 W. The redesigned wire uses one-quarter the power at the same voltage, not four times as much. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Original volume = AL = 0.50 mm²×0.80 m = 0.40 mm² m = 4.0×10⁻⁷ m³. Conservation gives A′L′ = AL, or A′ = AL/L′.
(ii) Let k = L′/L. Then A′ = A/k, so R′/R = (L′/L)(A/A′) = k² (1 mark). Here 1.00/0.25 = 4, so k = 2 (positive length), L′ = 1.60 m and A′ = 0.25 mm² (1 mark).
(iii) The design is feasible: 1.60 m ≤ the 1.70 m maximum, and 0.25 mm² ≥ the 0.20 mm² minimum. Both conditions must hold.
(iv) At fixed 2.0 V, P_original = 2.0²/0.25 = 16 W; P_new = 2.0²/1.00 = 4 W. The redesigned wire uses one-quarter the power at the same voltage, not four times as much.

questions.competency_rationale: Count the two-mark conserved-volume inverse design in (ii) and feasibility in (iii); direct volume and power calculations in (i)/(iv) are foundational.

questions.text:
A laboratory receives wires A and B. A has length 1.0 m and diameter 0.20 mm; B has length 2.0 m and diameter 0.40 mm. Separate tests at 1.2 V give currents 0.30 A in A and 0.60 A in B.
(i) Calculate the measured resistance of each wire. [1 mark]
(ii) Without needing π, determine the ratio of their resistivities. Explain why B’s lower resistance does not establish a better-conducting material. [2 marks]
(iii) The lab needs a 4.0 Ω resistor from stock of B’s material and diameter, with at most 3.0 m allowed. Determine whether it is possible with this stock unchanged. [1 mark]
(iv) If exactly 2.0 m must instead be used, specify the conducting area as a fraction of B’s area that would give 4.0 Ω. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Design from measured resistance and diameter
questions.answer:
(i) R_A = 1.2/0.30 = 4.0 Ω and R_B = 1.2/0.60 = 2.0 Ω (0.5 mark each). [1 mark]
(ii) Area_B/Area_A = (0.40/0.20)² = 4. Therefore ρ_B/ρ_A = (R_B/R_A)(Area_B/Area_A)(L_A/L_B) = (2/4)×4×(1/2) = 1 (1 mark). Equal resistivity means the lower measured resistance of B is explained by its fourfold area and doubled length, not by a lower-resistivity material (1 mark). [2 marks]
(iii) Unchanged B stock has 2.0 Ω per 2.0 m = 1.0 Ω/m. A 4.0 Ω piece requires 4.0 m, so it cannot meet the 3.0 m limit. [1 mark]
(iv) At fixed material and length 2.0 m, doubling resistance from 2.0 to 4.0 Ω requires half of B’s conducting area: Area_new = Area_B/2. This is a new wire specification, not unchanged stock. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Area_B/Area_A = (0.40/0.20)² = 4. Therefore ρ_B/ρ_A = (R_B/R_A)(Area_B/Area_A)(L_A/L_B) = (2/4)×4×(1/2) = 1 (1 mark). Equal resistivity means the lower measured resistance of B is explained by its fourfold area and doubled length, not by a lower-resistivity material (1 mark).
(iii) Unchanged B stock has 2.0 Ω per 2.0 m = 1.0 Ω/m. A 4.0 Ω piece requires 4.0 m, so it cannot meet the 3.0 m limit.
(iv) At fixed material and length 2.0 m, doubling resistance from 2.0 to 4.0 Ω requires half of B’s conducting area: Area_new = Area_B/2. This is a new wire specification, not unchanged stock.

questions.competency_rationale: Count geometry-normalised inference in (ii) and length-limit decision in (iii); direct resistance and fixed-length inverse-area scaling in (i)/(iv) are foundational.

questions.text:
Two candidate uniform resistive pads are to be formed separately from equal volumes, 4.0×10⁻⁷ m³, of the same alloy. Its operating resistivity is 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m. Candidate U has wire length 1.0 m; candidate V has wire length 2.0 m. Each candidate uses its entire allotted volume, without loss. Either pad would be connected directly across an ideal 10 V source. The source must supply no more than 2.0 A. A job requires 6000 J of useful heat within 700 s, and all electrical energy reaches the load.
(i) Find the conducting area and resistance of each candidate. [2 marks]
(ii) Find their currents and decide which meets the source-current limit. [1 mark]
(iii) Check whether the current-compatible candidate meets the time limit. [1 mark]
(iv) A seller claims the rejected, higher-power pad would use less electrical energy for the same job. Assess this claim under the stated assumptions. [1 mark]
questions.topic: Energy decision with a fixed wire volume
questions.answer:
(i) Area_U = volume/L_U = 4.0×10⁻⁷ m², and R_U = ρL_U/Area_U = 2.5 Ω (1 mark). Area_V = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m² and R_V = 1.0×10⁻⁶×2.0/(2.0×10⁻⁷) = 10 Ω (1 mark). The areas differ because the same material volume is distributed over different lengths. [2 marks]
(ii) I_U = 10/2.5 = 4.0 A, exceeding 2.0 A; I_V = 10/10 = 1.0 A, within the limit. Only V is current-compatible. [1 mark]
(iii) P_V = 10×1 = 10 W; t_V = 6000/10 = 600 s, which is below 700 s. V satisfies both operating requirements. [1 mark]
(iv) The claim is false in this loss-free model. Either pad transfers the required 6000 J and therefore consumes 6000 J = 1/600 kWh ≈ 0.00167 kWh for the job. U would be faster (40 W, 150 s) if an adequate source were used, but would not save task energy and is inadmissible on the given source. [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Area_U = volume/L_U = 4.0×10⁻⁷ m², and R_U = ρL_U/Area_U = 2.5 Ω (1 mark). Area_V = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m² and R_V = 1.0×10⁻⁶×2.0/(2.0×10⁻⁷) = 10 Ω (1 mark). The areas differ because the same material volume is distributed over different lengths.
(ii) I_U = 10/2.5 = 4.0 A, exceeding 2.0 A; I_V = 10/10 = 1.0 A, within the limit. Only V is current-compatible.
(iii) P_V = 10×1 = 10 W; t_V = 6000/10 = 600 s, which is below 700 s. V satisfies both operating requirements.

(iv) The claim is false in this loss-free model. Either pad transfers the required 6000 J and therefore consumes 6000 J = 1/600 kWh ≈ 0.00167 kWh for the job. U would be faster (40 W, 150 s) if an adequate source were used, but would not save task energy and is inadmissible on the given source.

questions.competency_rationale: Parts (i) use routine A = volume/L then R = ρL/A and receive no competency credit. Count current-limit decision (ii), deadline check (iii), and energy-claim evaluation (iv).

questions.text:
A class tests different lengths from one wire stock at constant temperature using two clamps. Unlike the general ideal-contact assumption, the two clamp contacts together contribute an unknown series resistance C. In the first two trials the stock has a uniform conducting area and material, and C stays unchanged. The measured total resistance (wire plus both contacts) is 4.0 Ω for 0.50 m and 10.0 Ω for 1.50 m. Connecting leads have negligible resistance. Treat the readings as exact. For these trials write total resistance as kL + C, where k is the wire resistance per metre.
(i) Use the difference between the trials to infer k, then find C. Explain why simply dividing either total resistance by its length would give a misleading k. [2 marks]
(ii) Predict the total resistance for 2.00 m if the uniform-stock and unchanged-contact model continues to apply. [1 mark]
(iii) The 2.00 m trial instead gives 15.0 Ω. Consider only two explanations: H1, the contacts now add 2.0 Ω extra at every length while the wire remains uniform; H2, the contacts are unchanged but the added segment from 1.50 m to 2.00 m has extra resistance. The contact condition can be held unchanged while returning to the same previously tested 0.50 m or 1.50 m portion, excluding the added 1.50–2.00 m segment. Specify one shorter-length repeat and its predicted reading under each explanation. Does the single 15.0 Ω reading alone select between H1 and H2? [1 mark]
questions.topic: Case study: separating wire resistance from contact resistance
questions.answer:
(i) Subtracting cancels the common contacts: 10.0 − 4.0 = k(1.50 − 0.50), so k = 6.0 Ω/m (1 mark). C = 4.0 − 6.0×0.50 = 1.0 Ω for the two contacts together. Dividing totals by length would give 8.0 Ω/m and 6.67 Ω/m because the fixed contact contribution is incorrectly included as wire resistance (1 mark for C and the misleading-ratio explanation). [2 marks]
(ii) Predicted total = 6.0×2.00 + 1.0 = 13.0 Ω. This is a conditional model prediction, not a measurement or proof that all lengths obey it. [1 mark]
(iii) Repeat 0.50 m while maintaining the contact condition of the 15.0 Ω trial. H1 predicts 6.0×0.50 + (1.0+2.0) = 6.0 Ω; H2 predicts the original 4.0 Ω because the suspect added segment is absent. Alternatively repeat 1.50 m: H1 predicts 12.0 Ω, H2 predicts 10.0 Ω. The single 15.0 Ω reading fits both explanations and does not distinguish them (0.5 mark for one repeat with both predictions; 0.5 mark for the non-uniqueness conclusion). [1 mark]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Subtracting cancels the common contacts: 10.0 − 4.0 = k(1.50 − 0.50), so k = 6.0 Ω/m (1 mark). C = 4.0 − 6.0×0.50 = 1.0 Ω for the two contacts together. Dividing totals by length would give 8.0 Ω/m and 6.67 Ω/m because the fixed contact contribution is incorrectly included as wire resistance (1 mark for C and the misleading-ratio explanation).
(ii) Predicted total = 6.0×2.00 + 1.0 = 13.0 Ω. This is a conditional model prediction, not a measurement or proof that all lengths obey it.

(iii) Repeat 0.50 m while maintaining the contact condition of the 15.0 Ω trial. H1 predicts 6.0×0.50 + (1.0+2.0) = 6.0 Ω; H2 predicts the original 4.0 Ω because the suspect added segment is absent. Alternatively repeat 1.50 m: H1 predicts 12.0 Ω, H2 predicts 10.0 Ω. The single 15.0 Ω reading fits both explanations and does not distinguish them (0.5 mark for one repeat with both predictions; 0.5 mark for the non-uniqueness conclusion).

questions.competency_rationale: Count two marks in (i) for difference-based cancellation of an unknown common series contribution and diagnosis of the length-ratio trap, plus (iii) for a discriminating repeat with competing predictions. The direct model prediction in (ii) is foundational.

questions.text:
A design team must make one continuous resistive track by cutting a uniform stock wire to a chosen path. The layout drawing supplies the two allowed paths and the minimum conducting area. It is not a circuit diagram: the two paths are alternatives and are never connected together. The wire’s operating resistivity is 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω m. The track is connected directly across 6.0 V, must draw no more than 1.2 A, and must deliver at least 360 J in 60 s. All electrical energy becomes useful heat. Only the two shown path lengths may be used; the conducting area may be chosen but must satisfy the drawing’s minimum.
(i) At the minimum permitted area, find the resistance of each path and reject any path that already draws too much current. [1 mark]
(ii) Can a permitted increase in conducting area rescue a path rejected in (i)? Explain. [1 mark]
(iii) For the remaining path at the minimum area, check both the source-current and heating requirements, and state a feasible design. [2 marks]
questions.topic: Case study: a constrained warming track
questions.answer:
(i) The drawing gives Area_min = 0.20 mm² = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m², path S = 0.80 m and path T = 1.20 m. R_S = 4.0 Ω and R_T = 6.0 Ω. At 6.0 V, I_S = 1.5 A > 1.2 A, so S is rejected; I_T = 1.0 A. [1 mark]
(ii) No. Increasing area decreases R = ρL/A and increases I at fixed voltage. Since S already draws too much current at the smallest permitted area, any permitted larger area makes that failure worse. [1 mark]
(iii) Choose path T with area 0.20 mm². Its current is 6/6 = 1.0 A ≤ 1.2 A (1 mark). Its heat in 60 s is H = VIt = 6×1×60 = 360 J, exactly the minimum, so this design meets both requirements (1 mark). [2 marks]

marking_scheme.step: (i) The drawing gives Area_min = 0.20 mm² = 2.0×10⁻⁷ m², path S = 0.80 m and path T = 1.20 m. R_S = 4.0 Ω and R_T = 6.0 Ω. At 6.0 V, I_S = 1.5 A > 1.2 A, so S is rejected; I_T = 1.0 A.

(ii) No. Increasing area decreases R = ρL/A and increases I at fixed voltage. Since S already draws too much current at the smallest permitted area, any permitted larger area makes that failure worse.

(iii) Choose path T with area 0.20 mm². Its current is 6/6 = 1.0 A ≤ 1.2 A (1 mark). Its heat in 60 s is H = VIt = 6×1×60 = 360 J, exactly the minimum, so this design meets both requirements (1 mark).

questions.competency_rationale: Count the rejection decision (i), monotonic rescue test (ii), and final heat/feasibility check (one mark in iii); repeating the already calculated current in (iii) earns no competency credit.

questions.text:
A 12 V laboratory station has two constant-resistance devices: a warming pad rated 12 V, 12 W and an indicator rated 12 V, 3 W. They must each receive 12 V when switched on. Each device has its own switch. In a daily session the pad runs for 20 minutes and the indicator for 1 hour; their operating periods may overlap. Assume an ideal 12 V supply, negligible switch/wire resistance, and no standby consumption.
(i) Choose series or parallel connection and explain how it meets both the voltage and independent-switching requirements. [1 mark]
(ii) Find the total source current when both devices are on. [1 mark]
(iii) A proposed operating schedule halves the pad’s daily on-time but leaves the indicator unchanged. Calculate the daily energy saved and the percentage reduction in the total daily electrical energy. [2 marks]
questions.topic: Case study: operating two tasks independently
questions.answer:
(i) Use parallel branches across the source, with a separate switch in series with each device within its branch. Each on-device receives 12 V, and opening one branch does not interrupt the other; a shared series path would not meet these requirements. [1 mark]
(ii) I_pad = 12 W/12 V = 1.0 A; I_indicator = 3 W/12 V = 0.25 A. The source supplies their sum, 1.25 A. [1 mark]
(iii) Original daily energy = 12×(20/60)+3×1 = 7 Wh. New daily energy = 12×(10/60)+3×1 = 5 Wh, so the saving is 2 Wh = 0.002 kWh = 7200 J (1 mark). Percentage saving = (2/7)×100 ≈ 28.6%, not 50%, because the indicator’s energy is unchanged (1 mark). [2 marks]

marking_scheme.step: (i) Use parallel branches across the source, with a separate switch in series with each device within its branch. Each on-device receives 12 V, and opening one branch does not interrupt the other; a shared series path would not meet these requirements.
(ii) I_pad = 12 W/12 V = 1.0 A; I_indicator = 3 W/12 V = 0.25 A. The source supplies their sum, 1.25 A.

(iii) Original daily energy = 12×(20/60)+3×1 = 7 Wh. New daily energy = 12×(10/60)+3×1 = 5 Wh, so the saving is 2 Wh = 0.002 kWh = 7200 J (1 mark). Percentage saving = (2/7)×100 ≈ 28.6%, not 50%, because the indicator’s energy is unchanged (1 mark).

questions.competency_rationale: Count topology choice with functional explanation (i) and total-baseline percentage interpretation (one mark in iii); current and saved-energy arithmetic are foundational.
